## Mediterranean Cruise Guide 2026: Everything You Need to Know Before You Book

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/croaziere/ghid-croaziere-mediterana
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** croaziere
**Publicat:** 2026-07-25
**Actualizat:** 2026-07-25

**Descriere:** Complete Mediterranean cruise guide for 2026. Real costs, what is included, which cruise line to choose, West vs East Med, best ports, when to book and what to avoid.

**Rezumat rapid:** A 7-night Mediterranean cruise costs between €399 and €900 per person depending on the cruise line, cabin type and season. The price includes accommodation, main meals and onboard entertainment. It does NOT include: alcoholic drinks, shore excursions, the mandatory gratuity (~€10–15/person/day), Wi-Fi, or flights to the embarkation port. Total realistic cost for two people for a week: €1,700–3,500 including flights, gratuities and a few excursions.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: What does the cruise price include?**
R: Typically included: accommodation in your cabin, main meals (breakfast, lunch, dinner at the buffet and main dining room), onboard entertainment (shows, pools, activities) and port access fees. NOT included: alcoholic beverages, specialty restaurants, organised shore excursions, spa treatments, Wi-Fi, the mandatory service charge (€10–15/person/day), and flights to the embarkation port.

**Î: When is the best time to book a Mediterranean cruise?**
R: Early booking (8–12 months ahead) gives the best prices and widest cabin selection. Peak season (July–August) costs 30–50% more than May–June or September. Last-minute deals can be exceptional but you lose control over dates and cabin category.

**Î: Interior cabin or balcony — is the price difference worth it?**
R: Depends on how you use the cabin. If you are rarely in your room (eating, sleeping, that is all), an interior cabin is excellent — you save €150–300 per person for the same itinerary. If you want morning coffee watching the sea or are doing a longer cruise, the balcony is worth the investment.

**Î: Which is better — Western or Eastern Mediterranean?**
R: Western Med (Spain, France, Italy) is ideal for a first cruise — large cities, easy logistics, cultural variety. Eastern Med (Greece, Croatia, Turkey) is better if you have done the west — spectacular islands, dramatic scenery, more exotic ports. Both are excellent; the choice depends on what you have already seen.

**Î: Which cruise line is best for first-timers?**
R: MSC and Costa are the classic first-cruise choices — European style, competitive prices, embarkation from Italian ports (short flight from most of Europe). Norwegian is excellent if you want more freedom and do not mind spending 30–50% more. Royal Caribbean is best for families with teenagers who want activities and thrill rides.

**Î: Are cruise shore excursions worth it?**
R: Ship-organised excursions are convenient (the ship waits for you if the tour runs late) but expensive — typically 2–3x the price of independent alternatives. For relaxed ports like Santorini or Dubrovnik, you can easily explore independently. For complex destinations like Pompeii or Ephesus, a guided excursion adds context that is hard to replicate on your own.

**Î: What is the mandatory gratuity and can I avoid it?**
R: Most cruise lines automatically add a service charge to your onboard account: approximately €10–15 per person per day. On a 7-night cruise for two people, that is €140–210. It is technically possible to request removal at Guest Services, but it is considered poor practice as it comes directly from the wages of cabin stewards and restaurant staff. Factor it into your budget from the start.

**Î: Is travel insurance necessary for a cruise?**
R: Yes — more so than for any other type of holiday. Cruise cancellation policies are the harshest in the travel industry (up to 100% forfeiture within 2 weeks of sailing). Medical repatriation from a cruise ship can be exceptionally complex and expensive. Travel insurance specifically noting 'cruise cover' is strongly recommended.

---

## Greece 2026 Holiday Guide: Which Island, Real Costs, When to Go and What to Know

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/city-breaks/greece-2026-holiday-guide
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** city-breaks
**Publicat:** 2026-07-29
**Actualizat:** 2026-07-29
**Traducere a:** [grecia-2026-ghid-vacanta](https://plecari.com/ro/city-breaks/grecia-2026-ghid-vacanta)

**Descriere:** Complete guide to a Greece holiday in 2026. Which island suits you, real prices by destination, how to get there, best beaches, car rental tips, and why September beats August.

**Rezumat rapid:** Greece is Europe's most popular summer destination in 2026, with Crete, Rhodes, Corfu, Santorini and Mykonos leading bookings. A 7-night holiday for two costs €750–3,500 depending on island and season. The sweet spot: Crete or Rhodes in September — same excellent weather, 20–30% lower prices, far fewer crowds. EU citizens need no visa. No eSIM needed (EU free roaming applies). A rental car is essential on large islands like Crete and Rhodes.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: Which Greek island is best for families with children?**
R: Crete is the best overall family destination — the largest island, varied beaches with safe shallow water, excellent all-inclusive options, good medical infrastructure, and plenty of non-beach activities (Minoan palaces, gorges, markets). Zakynthos and Rhodes are also strong family choices. Avoid Santorini and Mykonos with young children — the terrain is difficult, prices are extreme, and neither island is designed for family tourism.

**Î: Is September good for Greece?**
R: September is arguably the best month to visit Greece. Weather remains excellent (28–32°C air, 25°C sea temperature), the crowds reduce dramatically, prices drop 20–30% compared to August, and popular sites like Akrotiri in Santorini or the Palace of Knossos in Crete are actually enjoyable rather than overwhelming. The only downside: some seasonal restaurants and bars begin closing from mid-September.

**Î: Do I need a visa or eSIM for Greece?**
R: EU citizens need no visa — enter with a national ID card. Greece is in the EU, so free roaming applies — use your home mobile plan without extra charges. No eSIM needed for Greece specifically, though an eSIM is useful if your itinerary includes Turkey or other non-EU countries.

**Î: Is a rental car necessary in Greece?**
R: On large islands: essential. On Crete (250 km long) and Rhodes, the best beaches and villages are only reachable by car. On smaller islands (Mykonos, Paros, Zakynthos), ATVs or scooters are common alternatives. On Santorini and Hydra, cars are impractical or prohibited. See the full guide: car rental in Greece 2026.

**Î: What is the cheapest Greek island?**
R: For European travellers: Crete and Rhodes consistently offer the best value at the beach resort level — wide choice of all-inclusive hotels, direct flights from most European cities, and competitive prices. Lesbos, Samos, and Kos are cheaper but less frequently served. Santorini and Mykonos are in a category of their own — significantly more expensive than all other islands.

**Î: How much does a meal cost in Greece?**
R: A full meal at a local taverna (Greek salad + grilled fish or meat + wine) costs €15–25/person. Beach clubs and tourist-facing restaurants on Santorini, Mykonos, and the most popular resort areas charge €30–50/person. The best value: inland tavernas a few streets back from the main waterfront, particularly in Crete and Rhodes, where the food is better and the prices much lower.

**Î: Can I do a cruise of the Greek islands instead of staying on one island?**
R: Yes, and it is often excellent value. A 7-night Greek island cruise visits Santorini, Mykonos, Crete, and Rhodes or other islands — staying on the ship each night, spending 6–8 hours in each port. Costs: from €450/person for a cabin on MSC or Costa. For a comparison of cruising vs island stay, see the Mediterranean cruise guide.

## Greek Islands Cruise 2026: Santorini, Mykonos, Crete — Complete Guide with Real Prices

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/croaziere/greek-islands-cruise-2026
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** croaziere
**Publicat:** 2026-07-29
**Actualizat:** 2026-07-29
**Traducere a:** [croaziera-insulele-grecesti-2026](https://plecari.com/ro/croaziere/croaziera-insulele-grecesti-2026)

**Descriere:** Everything you need for Greek islands cruise in 2026. Itineraries, best cruise lines, real costs, how to get there, what to do at each port, and the Santorini overtourism restrictions you need to know

**Rezumat rapid:** A 7-night Greek islands cruise starts from €499–600 per person in an interior cabin (Costa or MSC), embarking from Athens (Piraeus), Bari or Ravenna. Classic itineraries visit Santorini, Mykonos, Crete (Heraklion), and Rhodes, with all main meals included. Add flights from your home country (€100–250 return), the mandatory service charge (~€70 per person for 7 nights), and optional shore excursions (€40–100 per port). Best season: May–June or September–October — lower prices, fewer crowds, same excellent weather.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: How much does a 7-night Greek islands cruise cost?**
R: Base cabin prices start from €499–600/person (interior cabin, Costa or MSC). Add: flights to the embarkation port (€100–250 return from most of Europe), mandatory service charge (€70/person for 7 nights at €10/day), optional drinks (€100–250 if not buying a package), shore excursions (€40–100 per port independently), and travel insurance (€25–50). Realistic all-in budget for two people: €1,700–2,800.

**Î: Which cruise line is best for Greek islands?**
R: MSC and Costa offer the best value for Greek island itineraries with the most departure options from Italian and Greek ports. Norwegian is better if you prioritise flexible dining. For a first cruise in the Greek islands, MSC from Civitavecchia (Rome) or Athens is the most accessible option. Celebrity Cruises offers premium Greek island itineraries with superior food quality.

**Î: Is Santorini still worth visiting on a cruise in 2026?**
R: Yes, but with caveats. Santorini has imposed daily limits on cruise passengers — some ships are now diverted in August. If your itinerary guarantees Santorini, the port stop is spectacular. If it says 'subject to availability', plan for the possibility of visiting Milos or Folegandros instead. September sailings have significantly fewer restrictions and a better experience.

**Î: Where do Greek island cruises embark?**
R: The most popular embarkation ports for Greek island cruises are Athens/Piraeus (closest to the islands, 1.5h direct flight from most European capitals), Bari (Southern Italy), Ravenna (near Venice), and Civitavecchia (Rome). Athens is the most convenient for itineraries focused on the eastern Mediterranean and Greek islands specifically.

**Î: Can I explore Greek islands independently without the cruise ship excursions?**
R: Yes, and it's significantly cheaper. At Santorini: cable car up and walk to Oia (free). At Mykonos: walk from the port into town and beach (free). At Crete: local bus to archaeological sites (€3–8 each way) plus €15–20 entrance. Ship excursions cost €50–120 per port for essentially the same content you can do independently for €15–25.

**Î: What is the best month for a Greek islands cruise?**
R: May–June is the best combination of weather, price, and experience. Sea temperatures reach 22–24°C (warm enough to swim), air temperatures 25–28°C, prices 15–25% lower than August, and crowds are manageable. September is equally excellent. July–August is peak season — hottest, most expensive, and most crowded, with Santorini restrictions in effect.

**Î: Do I need a visa or eSIM for a Greek islands cruise?**
R: EU citizens need no visa — Greece is an EU member state. The EHIC covers medical emergencies at Greek public hospitals. No eSIM needed within Greece. However, if your itinerary includes Turkey (Ephesus/Kusadasi), Turkey is non-EU — buy an eSIM before departure, as provider websites are blocked inside Turkey since 2025.

## Hidden Holiday Fees 2026: Every Cost Nobody Tells You About Before You Book

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/zboruri/hidden-holiday-fees-2026
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** zboruri
**Publicat:** 2026-07-31
**Actualizat:** 2026-07-31
**Traducere a:** [taxe-ascunse-vacanta-2026](https://plecari.com/ro/zboruri/taxe-ascunse-vacanta-2026)

**Descriere:** The complete guide to hidden fees in European travel — low-cost airline surcharges, hotel tourist taxes, DCC at ATMs, resort fees, car rental extras, and how to avoid or budget for each one.

**Rezumat rapid:** Hidden costs can add €100–400 to a holiday budget you thought was settled. The main culprits: low-cost airline baggage supplements (€25–100 per direction), hotel tourist tax not shown on Booking.com (€2–7/night), Dynamic Currency Conversion at ATMs and card terminals (3–8% loss on every transaction), car rental counter extras (CDW excess, insurance upgrades: €70–175/week), data roaming outside the EU (€3–12/day), and service charges added automatically to restaurant bills. The rule: always add 15–20% above the headline price.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: What fees are NOT included in hotel prices on Booking.com?**
R: The local tourist tax (€2–7/night depending on city and hotel category) is NOT included in the displayed price on Booking.com. You pay it at check-in, in cash or by card. Barcelona, Amsterdam, Rome, Venice, Paris, Lisbon — all have compulsory tourist taxes that appear only in the fine print or at check-in. Some hotels also charge resort fees (especially in Turkey and Egypt) at check-in that weren't visible at booking.

**Î: How do I avoid losing money at ATMs abroad?**
R: Always choose to pay in the LOCAL CURRENCY, never in your home currency. Dynamic Currency Conversion (DCC) is a mechanism where the ATM or payment terminal makes the conversion at an exchange rate 3–8% worse than your bank's rate. If the screen asks 'pay in pounds or euros?' — choose euros. If it asks 'conversion by ATM or your bank?' — choose your bank.

**Î: Why is my actual holiday spend always more than what I planned?**
R: Because headline prices exclude most of the real costs: the Ryanair 'from €25' doesn't include your bag; the hotel 'from €60' doesn't include the tourist tax; the 'free' city WiFi doesn't cover your roaming in Turkey; and that nice restaurant lunch came with a 12.5% service charge and a €2/person cover charge. Adding 15–20% to every headline price before booking gives a realistic picture.

**Î: How much does Dynamic Currency Conversion actually cost?**
R: 3–8% on every transaction where you choose your home currency instead of the local one. On a holiday with €800 of card spending, DCC costs €24–64. On €2,000 (a family holiday), it's €60–160. Use Revolut or Wise (0% exchange fee) and always choose local currency, and this cost drops to zero.

**Î: What car rental fees appear at the counter that aren't in the online price?**
R: The most common surprise fees at the rental counter: CDW excess reduction (€10–15/day, sometimes mandatory), additional driver fee (€5–15/day), young driver surcharge (under 25), airport collection surcharge (€5–20), fuel policy pre-purchase (often non-refundable), tyre/glass/roof protection (€3–8/day each). Total: €70–175 for a 7-day rental. Buy comprehensive insurance when booking online — it's cheaper and prevents most of this.

**Î: What tourist taxes are applied in Europe's top destinations in 2026?**
R: The biggest tourist taxes in 2026: Amsterdam (16% on room rate — the highest), Barcelona (€4–6.75/night), Rome (€3.50–7/night), Venice (€5–10/day for day visitors plus per-night hotel tax), Paris (€1–5/night), Lisbon (€2/night), Dubrovnik (€2/night). These are all mandatory, non-avoidable, and frequently not shown on Booking.com at search time.

**Î: Is the 'airport tax' included in flight prices shown on comparison engines?**
R: Usually yes — EU regulations require that the final price including taxes and charges be shown in search results. But 'optional' charges (baggage, seat selection, priority boarding) are added separately. The advertised base fare and the realistic all-in price for a passenger with a bag can differ by €50–150 per direction on low-cost airlines.

## How to Find Cheap Accommodation in 2026: 12 Strategies That Actually Work

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/cazari/how-to-find-cheap-accommodation
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** cazari
**Publicat:** 2026-07-30
**Actualizat:** 2026-07-30
**Traducere a:** [cum-gasesti-cazare-ieftina](https://plecari.com/ro/cazari/cum-gasesti-cazare-ieftina)

**Descriere:** How to find cheap accommodation: when to book, which platforms to compare, the zone strategy that saves 30–50%, hidden costs to check before confirming, and how to read reviews.

**Rezumat rapid:** The most effective strategies for cheap accommodation: book early with free cancellation and re-book if the price drops; compare at least 3 sources (Booking, the hotel's own website, and one alternative platform); stay in zone 2–3 of the city (30–50% cheaper with identical experience); choose apartments with kitchens for groups or stays over 5 nights; avoid peak season. On a 5-night trip for two people, these adjustments save €100–250 compared to booking impulsively on the first platform that appears.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: Is it cheaper to book directly with the hotel or through Booking.com?**
R: It depends. Booking.com charges hotels a 15–25% commission. Many independent hotels pass some of this back to direct bookers as a 5–15% discount on their own website. Large chains (Marriott, Hilton, IHG) typically have identical prices everywhere. The practical rule: always check the hotel's own website after checking Booking — 2 minutes that can save €10–25/night.

**Î: Should I book accommodation early or last-minute?**
R: For popular destinations in peak season (Mediterranean in July–August, ski resorts in February): book early with free cancellation, then set a price alert and rebook if it drops. Last-minute works for off-season travel or less popular destinations where hotels prefer partial revenue to empty rooms. Never wait last-minute for Greece in August or Dubrovnik in July.

**Î: When does an apartment make more sense than a hotel?**
R: For groups of 3 or more (cost splits across everyone), for stays of 5+ nights (kitchen saves €15–30/day on meals), and for families with children (space and flexibility). For 1–2 people on a 2–3 night city break, a budget hotel is typically comparable or cheaper with less logistical complexity.

**Î: What hidden costs should I check before confirming accommodation?**
R: Always check: local tourist tax (€1–10+/person/night — not shown in displayed price on all platforms), resort/city fee (€5–25/night at resort hotels), parking (€10–30/night at central hotels), breakfast if not included (€10–20/person), and Airbnb cleaning fee (€30–80 per stay, not in the per-night price).

**Î: Is Airbnb still worth using in 2026?**
R: For apartments: yes, with caveats. In major European cities, stricter short-term rental regulations have reduced supply and pushed prices up. Booking.com Apartments and Vrbo often list the same properties without the cleaning fee surprise. Always compare the total price (nightly rate × nights + cleaning fee) rather than the per-night headline price.

**Î: What is a good Booking.com score and how reliable are reviews?**
R: 8.0+ is generally reliable; 8.5+ for confidence; 9.0+ is excellent. But always sort by 'Most Recent' — a hotel with an 8.7 overall but recent reviews of 6.0 has degraded since the score was built. Look for specific mentions of cleanliness, noise, Wi-Fi, and whether the location matches what the map shows.

**Î: What is the Booking.com Genius programme?**
R: Genius is Booking.com's free loyalty programme. Level 1 (2 completed bookings): 10% discount at participating properties. Level 2 (5 bookings): 15% discount plus early check-in and late check-out. Levels do not expire. If you book 2+ hotels per year, Genius adds 10–15% savings at no cost.

**Î: Are hostels worth it for adults, not just students?**
R: Private rooms in well-rated social hostels are excellent value at any age: €25–50/night with communal areas (bar, kitchen, organised events) that make solo travel less isolating. Dormitory beds (€8–20/night) are the cheapest accommodation available. Key threshold: 8.5+ on Hostelworld consistently means adequate cleanliness and a reasonable atmosphere.

## How to Install an eSIM on iPhone or Android: Step-by-Step Guide 2026

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/esim-roaming/how-to-install-esim
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** esim-roaming
**Publicat:** 2026-07-29
**Actualizat:** 2026-07-29
**Traducere a:** [cum-instalezi-esim](https://plecari.com/ro/esim-roaming/cum-instalezi-esim)

**Descriere:** Exact steps to install an eSIM on iPhone and Android, which phones support it, common errors and fixes, and how to set up dual SIM so you keep your regular number while using local data.

**Rezumat rapid:** Installing an eSIM takes 2–3 minutes: buy a plan from a provider like Airalo or Saily, receive a QR code by email, go to your phone's SIM or mobile data settings, select 'Add eSIM', scan the QR code, and the profile downloads automatically. Do this at home on a stable Wi-Fi connection before your trip. The eSIM sits dormant until you land and activate it — your regular SIM stays active for calls and SMS the entire time.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: Does my phone support eSIM?**
R: iPhone: XS, XR and all newer models (from 2018). iPhone 6, 7, 8, and X do not have eSIM. Samsung: Galaxy S20 and newer, Z Fold/Flip series. Google Pixel: 3 and newer. Quick check: dial *#06# — if an 'EID' code appears in the list, your phone supports eSIM. On iPhone: Settings → General → About → look for 'EID'. On Android: Settings → Connections or Network → if 'Add eSIM' appears, you have support.

**Î: Do I need Wi-Fi to install an eSIM?**
R: Yes. The phone downloads the eSIM profile from the provider's servers, which requires an internet connection. Install at home on your own Wi-Fi before the trip. If you are already abroad without data, you can install via a hotel or café Wi-Fi, but it is much simpler to do it in advance.

**Î: Can the QR code be scanned more than once?**
R: No. Most eSIM QR codes are single-use — once scanned and the profile installed, the code is deactivated. If you scan it and the installation fails (poor Wi-Fi, phone restart mid-process), contact the provider. Most will issue a new code for free for genuine installation failures.

**Î: How do I activate the eSIM when I land?**
R: The eSIM profile is installed but inactive until you turn it on. When you land: go to Settings → Mobile Data (iPhone) or Connections → SIM Manager (Android) → select your eSIM profile → enable it as the data SIM. Also ensure 'Data Roaming' is enabled on the eSIM profile — without this, the eSIM connects to partner networks but no data flows.

**Î: Can I keep my regular number while using an eSIM?**
R: Yes — that is the primary advantage of eSIM. Your physical SIM stays active for calls, SMS, and bank verification codes. The eSIM handles data. Both work simultaneously with dual SIM. Set data to the eSIM, calls and SMS to your physical SIM, and you have the best of both: local data rates and your regular number.

**Î: What if my phone is carrier-locked?**
R: A carrier-locked phone cannot use SIM cards from other operators, including eSIM profiles. eSIM support and being carrier-unlocked are separate requirements — you need both. Contact your carrier to unlock the phone (usually free after the contract period ends). Note: this does not apply to carrier-locked eSIM functionality — if your carrier has locked eSIM access, it needs to be unlocked separately.

**Î: Can I use an eSIM in Turkey?**
R: Yes, but you must buy and install it BEFORE arriving in Turkey. Since 2025, Turkish authorities block access to major eSIM provider websites (Airalo, Saily) from within Turkey. The eSIM profile installed at home works normally once you land in Istanbul or Antalya.

**Î: How long does an eSIM plan last?**
R: Plans are typically sold with a fixed data allowance and a validity period: for example, 5 GB valid for 30 days from activation. The plan expires when you use all the data OR when the validity period ends — whichever comes first. Some providers offer 'top up' options if you run out of data before the period ends.

## How to Plan a European Holiday from Scratch: Step-by-Step Guide 2026

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/zboruri/how-to-plan-european-holiday-2026
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** zboruri
**Publicat:** 2026-07-15
**Actualizat:** 2026-07-15
**Traducere a:** [cum-planifici-vacanta-ghid-pas-cu-pas](https://plecari.com/ro/zboruri/cum-planifici-vacanta-ghid-pas-cu-pas)

**Descriere:** The complete planning checklist for a European holiday in 2026. From choosing a destination to packing your bag — flights, accommodation, insurance, eSIM, documents, and timing.

**Rezumat rapid:** Plan a European holiday in 7 steps: 1) Set budget and destination (3-6 months ahead). 2) Book flights (6-8 weeks ahead for best price). 3) Book accommodation. 4) Get travel insurance (€15-25/week). 5) Buy an eSIM for data (€5-15). 6) Check documents (passport, ETA for UK, EHIC card). 7) Pack. The entire process takes 2-3 hours if you know what you're doing — this guide shows you exactly what and when.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: How far in advance should I book a European holiday?**
R: Flights: 6-8 weeks ahead for the best price. Accommodation: 2-3 months (4-6 months for peak season or popular destinations). Insurance: as soon as you make your first non-refundable booking. Popular attraction tickets (Colosseum, Sagrada Familia): 2-4 weeks ahead.

**Î: How much does a European holiday cost per person?**
R: Varies enormously. City break (3 nights): £200-650. Beach holiday (7 nights): €400-1,200. Cruise (7 nights): $800-2,500. The cheapest destinations (Budapest, Bucharest, Athens) cost €40-60/day; expensive ones (London, Amsterdam, Paris) cost €80-150/day.

**Î: Do I need travel insurance for Europe?**
R: EHIC/GHIC covers emergency treatment at public EU hospitals, but NOT repatriation, cancellation, lost baggage, or private hospitals. A dedicated policy costs £15-30/week — less than a single restaurant meal — and covers everything EHIC doesn't. For non-EU destinations (Turkey, UK), insurance is essential.

## Car Rental in Greece 2026: Documents, Prices, Rules and Island-by-Island Guide

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/inchirieri-auto/inchiriere-masina-grecia-2026
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** inchirieri-auto
**Publicat:** 2026-07-25
**Actualizat:** 2026-07-25

**Descriere:** Everything you need to know before renting a car in Greece: required documents, 2026 traffic law changes, real prices by season, which islands need a car and which traps to avoid.

**Rezumat rapid:** EU citizens can rent a car in Greece with their EU driving licence — no international permit required. Minimum age is 21, with a young driver surcharge for under-25s. A credit card is required for the deposit. Key 2026 change: speed limits in urban areas have dropped to 30 km/h with stricter enforcement and higher fines. On large islands (Crete, Rhodes), a rental car is practically essential to reach the best beaches and villages.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: Do I need an international driving permit for Greece?**
R: No, if you hold an EU driving licence. EU licences are recognised directly across all member states. An international driving permit is only required for drivers from outside the EU (USA, UK, Australia, etc.) or when the licence is not written in Latin characters.

**Î: What credit cards do Greek rental companies accept?**
R: Typically Visa or Mastercard credit cards in the driver's name, used for the security deposit hold. Debit cards are accepted less frequently and with additional conditions. Revolut can work if you have the credit card version (not prepaid or debit). Always verify before booking — especially with small local companies on smaller islands, which sometimes insist on a traditional credit card.

**Î: Should I bring my own car or rent locally?**
R: Depends on the destination. For Halkidiki or Thassos (reachable by road), your own car works well. For Crete, Rhodes, Corfu, or Zakynthos (reached by flight), rent locally — it is far cheaper and simpler than paying €100–200 each way to ship your car on a ferry.

**Î: What is the average car rental price in Greece in peak season?**
R: A small hatchback (Hyundai i10, VW Polo) costs €35–70/day in July–August on the islands. Prices drop 20–30% in May–June and September. Booking 4–6 weeks ahead typically saves 25–40% compared to walk-up prices at the island airport.

**Î: What happens if I scratch the car?**
R: If CDW (Collision Damage Waiver) is included, the company covers the damage minus the excess (which can be €500–1,500). If you have not reduced the excess to zero, you pay that amount. Always photograph the car thoroughly at collection — every existing scratch, on all four sides, roof included — and email the photos to yourself immediately as timestamped proof.

**Î: Can I drive between Greek islands with a rental car?**
R: No. Rental contracts in Greece are almost always restricted to the island or region where you collected the car. Taking the vehicle on a ferry to another island is specifically prohibited by most rental agreements. If you want to visit multiple islands, you return the car, take a ferry or flight, and rent again at the next island.

**Î: Is a GPS or a phone sufficient for navigation in Greece?**
R: Your phone with Google Maps is completely sufficient. Download the offline map for the island before departure. The counter GPS (€8–15/day) is an unnecessary expense. Road signs in Greece are bilingual (Greek and Latin alphabet) on main roads, so navigation is manageable even without a device — but GPS helps on the narrow backroads of Crete or Corfu.

## Interrail 2026: The Complete Guide to Train Travel Across Europe

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/zboruri/interrail-europe-2026-complete-guide
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** zboruri
**Publicat:** 2026-07-14
**Actualizat:** 2026-07-14

**Descriere:** Everything you need to know about Interrail in 2026. Pass prices, best routes, night trains, seat reservations, and whether a rail pass actually saves you money.

**Rezumat rapid:** An Interrail Global Pass in 2026 starts at €212 (youth, 4 days/1 month) or €330 (adult). A full month of unlimited travel: €522 adults. The pass covers 33 European countries. Night trains (Nightjet: Vienna-Rome, Munich-Amsterdam) save hotel nights. Key caveat: high-speed trains (TGV, Frecciarossa, AVE) require paid seat reservations (€10-34 per segment) on top of the pass. Best value: 5+ cities in 2-4 weeks, youth pass, shoulder season.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: How much does an Interrail Global Pass cost in 2026?**
R: 2nd class prices — Youth (12-27): 4 days/1 month = €212, 7 days = €268, 1 month continuous = €522. Adult (28-59): 4 days = €330, 7 days = €414, 1 month = €713. Senior (60+): ~10% discount. Children under 12: FREE with a paying adult (max 2 children).

**Î: Do I need seat reservations with Interrail?**
R: Depends on the train. Regional trains (Germany, Austria, Czech Republic, Switzerland): NO, just board. High-speed trains: YES, mandatory — TGV France (€10-20), Frecciarossa Italy (€13), AVE Spain, Eurostar (€34). Night trains (Nightjet): YES — seats from €14, couchettes from €34. Book at interrail.eu or at the station.

**Î: Is Interrail cheaper than flying?**
R: For 2-3 fixed cities: usually not — budget flights are cheaper. For 5+ cities with flexibility: Interrail wins, especially for under-27s (€212 for 4 travel days = ~€53/day). Plus: no baggage fees, you arrive in city centres (not airports 30-80 km away), and the scenery is spectacular.

**Î: Can I use Interrail on night trains?**
R: Yes, but you must pay a compulsory berth or seat reservation. Nightjet (ÖBB) is the main operator: Vienna-Rome, Vienna-Venice, Munich-Amsterdam, Zurich-Hamburg, Vienna-Paris. Reservations: seats from ~€14, couchettes from ~€34, private sleepers higher. Book the moment reservations open (typically 3-6 months ahead) — cheap berths sell out in days on popular routes.

## Is Romania Expensive? Real Travel Costs in 2026

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/city-breaks/is-romania-expensive
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** city-breaks
**Publicat:** 2026-07-09
**Traducere a:** [romania-scumpa-ghid](https://plecari.com/ro/city-breaks/romania-scumpa-ghid)

**Descriere:** An honest cost breakdown for visiting Romania in 2026 — meals, hotels, transport, and activities with actual prices from someone who lives here.

**Rezumat rapid:** Romania is one of the most affordable countries in the EU. A comfortable mid-range day in Bucharest costs around €60–80 per person (hotel, meals, transport, one activity). Budget travelers can manage on €30–40/day. Outside the capital, costs drop further — a pension in Transylvania with breakfast runs €25–40 per night for a double room.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: How much does a meal cost in Romania?**
R: A full meal at a local restaurant costs €6–10. A coffee is €1.50–2.50. A three-course dinner at a mid-range restaurant runs €15–25 per person. Fast food is €4–6. Street food like covrigi (pretzels) costs under €1.

**Î: Is Bucharest cheaper than other European capitals?**
R: Significantly. Bucharest is roughly 40–50% cheaper than Prague, 50–60% cheaper than Vienna, and about half the cost of Barcelona or Rome for equivalent experiences. Only Sofia and Belgrade are comparably cheap among European capitals.

**Î: Do I need cash or can I pay by card?**
R: Card payments are widely accepted in cities — restaurants, supermarkets, taxis, and most attractions take Visa and Mastercard. In rural areas and small villages, carry some cash (Romanian leu, RON). ATMs are everywhere in cities.

**Î: How much should I budget per day in Romania?**
R: Budget: €30–40/day (hostel, local food, public transport). Mid-range: €60–80/day (3-star hotel, restaurants, occasional taxi). Comfort: €100–150/day (4-star hotel, car rental, guided tours). These are per-person estimates.

**Î: Is it cheaper to visit Romania in winter?**
R: Accommodation outside ski resorts is cheaper in the off-season (November–March, excluding Christmas/New Year). However, Romania's best value is actually in spring (April–June) and early autumn (September–October) — pleasant weather, fewer tourists, and no peak-season surcharges.

**Î: How much does a rental car cost in Romania?**
R: A compact car rents for €20–35 per day including basic insurance. Fuel costs around €1.50–1.70 per liter. Renting a car is the best way to explore Transylvania, Maramureș, and the Danube Delta at your own pace.

## Istanbul City Break 2026: 3-Day Itinerary, Real Costs and Everything You Need to Know

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/city-breaks/istanbul-city-break-guide
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** city-breaks
**Publicat:** 2026-07-29
**Actualizat:** 2026-07-29
**Traducere a:** [istanbul-city-break-ghid](https://plecari.com/ro/city-breaks/istanbul-city-break-ghid)

**Descriere:** Complete Istanbul city break guide for 2026. Hagia Sophia, Grand Bazaar, Bosphorus cruise, Turkish hammam, best neighbourhoods, real budget, and the eSIM you must buy before you fly.

**Rezumat rapid:** A 3-night Istanbul city break costs €250–550 per person all-in (flight + hotel + food + sites). Istanbul is one of Europe's most affordable city break destinations: a full meal costs €5–10, a Bosphorus ferry €1–2, and most major mosques are free. Essential to know before travelling: Turkey is not in the EU, so roaming applies — buy an eSIM before you fly (provider websites are blocked inside Turkey since 2025). Travel insurance is mandatory — the EHIC does not work in Turkey.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: How many days do you need in Istanbul?**
R: 3 days covers the essentials: Day 1 for Sultanahmet (Hagia Sophia, Blue Mosque, Topkapi Palace, Basilica Cistern), Day 2 for the Grand Bazaar, Galata district and Bosphorus, Day 3 for Kadıköy on the Asian side and a Turkish hammam. 4–5 days lets you add the Prince's Islands, Balat neighbourhood, and more food exploration. Even 2 full days produces a rewarding trip if you prioritise ruthlessly.

**Î: Is Istanbul safe for tourists in 2026?**
R: Yes. Istanbul is a safe city for tourists. Standard urban precautions apply: watch for pickpockets at the Grand Bazaar and on the T1 tram, use Bolt or Uber rather than unlicensed taxis, and be wary of unsolicited invitations to 'my friend's bar' (a well-documented scam where the bill arrives at €100–200+). The tourist police in Sultanahmet are responsive and helpful.

**Î: Do I need a visa for Istanbul?**
R: Most Western nationalities (UK, US, Canada, Australia, most EU countries) can enter Turkey without a visa for up to 90 days — but check your specific nationality at the Turkish Ministry of Foreign Affairs website, as requirements vary. Your passport must be valid for at least 6 months from your entry date. National ID cards are NOT accepted in Turkey.

**Î: Do I need an eSIM for Istanbul?**
R: Yes, strongly recommended — and buy it before you fly. Turkey is not in the EU, so free roaming does not apply. Carrier roaming costs €10–15/GB. A 5 GB Turkey eSIM costs approximately $10–15 on Airalo. Critical: since 2025, Turkish authorities block access to eSIM provider websites from within Turkey. You cannot purchase after arrival — the websites simply do not load.

**Î: What is the Museum Pass Istanbul and is it worth it?**
R: The Museum Pass Istanbul (approximately €55–65 for 5 days) covers 12 major sites including Topkapi Palace, Hagia Sophia Museum section, Chora Church, Dolmabahçe Palace, and several others. If you plan to visit Topkapi (€20) + Hagia Sophia Museum (entry charges for non-prayer access) + Dolmabahçe (€25+), the pass pays for itself. Valid for 5 consecutive days.

**Î: What currency should I use in Istanbul?**
R: Turkish lira (TRY). In tourist areas and large restaurants, euros and US dollars are sometimes accepted but at poor rates. Withdraw TRY from ATMs (not at the airport — rates are poor there). Use Revolut or Wise for card payments to avoid foreign transaction fees. Always refuse DCC (Dynamic Currency Conversion) — choose Turkish lira at every terminal. For the full payment guide: how to pay abroad without fees.

**Î: What is a Turkish hammam and which one should I choose?**
R: A Turkish hammam (bath house) involves a steam room, exfoliating scrub (kese), and soap massage. The experience typically takes 45–90 minutes. For a first visit: Çemberlitaş Hamamı (€40–80, open since 1584, central location), Süleymaniye Hamamı (€30–50, more local atmosphere), or Kılıç Ali Paşa Hamamı (€80–120, the most beautifully restored). Book online to guarantee a slot.

## Lake Como 2026: The Complete Guide — Bellagio, Varenna, Villas, Ferry & Everything You Need to Know

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/city-breaks/lake-como-complete-guide-2026
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** city-breaks
**Publicat:** 2026-07-31
**Actualizat:** 2026-07-31

**Descriere:** Lake Como 2026 complete guide. Bellagio vs Varenna vs Menaggio, ferry routes, famous villas, real prices and how to visit without the crowds.

**Rezumat rapid:** Lake Como (Lago di Como) is a Y-shaped glacial lake in the foothills of the Alps in Lombardy, northern Italy — 46 km long, up to 410 metres deep (the third deepest lake in Europe), surrounded by mountains rising to 2,400 metres. The central triangle of Bellagio, Varenna, and Menaggio is the heart of any Lake Como visit. Best access from Milan: train to Varenna (1 hour from Milano Centrale, €8.70 — gets you directly to the lake and the ferries). Ferry system operated by Navigazione Laghi: central car ferry Bellagio–Varenna–Menaggio every 20–30 minutes; fares increased ~15% for 2026. Villa del Balbianello (Casino Royale, Star Wars filming location): gardens €14, guided tour €25, open mid-March to end of December, closed Monday and Wednesday. Best time: May–June and September–October.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: How do you get from Milan to Lake Como?**
R: The best option depends on your destination. For Varenna (the best village for direct train access): Milano Centrale → Varenna-Esino on the Lecco regional line, 1 hour, €8.70. You step off the train and are immediately at the lake and the ferry pier — no further connections needed. For Como city: Milano Nord (Cadorna) → Como Nord via the Ferrovie Nord line, 35–40 minutes, €5. Then ferry from Como to the villages. From Milan Linate airport: taxi to Milano Centrale (15–20 min), then train as above. From Milan Malpensa: train to Milano Centrale (40 min), then as above.

**Î: Bellagio, Varenna, or Menaggio — which is the best base on Lake Como?**
R: Each suits different visitors. Bellagio: the most famous and most beautiful, on the central promontory where the two lake branches meet, with both Villa Serbelloni and Villa Melzi gardens. Most crowded, most expensive, books out months ahead in summer. Best for: first-timers, couples wanting the iconic experience. Varenna: smaller, less crowded, directly train-accessible from Milan, with Villa Monastero gardens and Castello di Vezio above. Best for: those arriving by train, quiet atmosphere, value. Menaggio: on the western shore, same ferry access as Bellagio across the central triangle, a free public lido beach, flatter streets (good for families). Best for: families, those wanting flexibility and more accommodation options.

**Î: How does the Lake Como ferry work?**
R: Navigazione Laghi operates all public ferries. Three types: slow ferry (traghetto — stops at all villages, best for sightseeing, bicycles allowed), hydrofoil (aliscafo — faster, no stops, no bicycles, slightly more expensive), and car ferry (traghetto auto — the only service carrying vehicles, runs the central triangle Bellagio–Varenna–Menaggio–Cadenabbia continuously every 20–30 minutes). Fares increased ~15% for 2026 vs 2025. Key prices: Como to Bellagio slow ferry €12.40, hydrofoil €18.80. Central lake crossing (Bellagio–Varenna): €4.60. Day pass for central lake: check navigazionelaghi.it. Tickets at piers or on the slower ferries; hydrofoil tickets must be purchased before boarding.

**Î: What is Villa del Balbianello and why is it so famous?**
R: Villa del Balbianello is an 18th-century villa on a wooded promontory jutting into the western branch of Lake Como near Lenno. Built for Cardinal Angelo Maria Durini in the late 1700s, later owned and transformed by Italian explorer Guido Monzino (who donated it to FAI, Italy's heritage trust, in 1988). Famous beyond Italy for two films: Star Wars: Episode II — Attack of the Clones (2002), where the terraced gardens served as Anakin and Padmé's lakeside retreat; and Casino Royale (2006), where Bond recovers with Vesper Lynd under the Loggia Durini after the torture scene. The Daily Telegraph called it 'the undisputed queen of all Bond film locations.' Entry 2026: gardens only €14, gardens + guided tour €25. Closed Monday and Wednesday.

**Î: Is Lake Como worth visiting for just one day from Milan?**
R: Yes — one day gives you a meaningful experience if planned well. The optimal day trip: 08:35 train from Milano Centrale to Varenna (arrive 09:35), ferry to Bellagio (15 min), explore Bellagio and Villa Melzi gardens (3–4 hours), ferry to Menaggio for lunch (20 min), ferry back across to Varenna (10 min), Castello di Vezio (45 min uphill), train back to Milan (last direct around 20:00). The mistake is spending all day in Como town — the city is less interesting than the villages, and it's the wrong end of the lake from the scenery.

**Î: When is the best time to visit Lake Como?**
R: May and September are the golden months: wildflowers on the hillsides (May), vineyards changing colour (September), ferry at full schedule, villas open, temperatures 18–24°C and 22–26°C respectively, accommodation 20–30% below summer peak. June is excellent. July–August: hot (28–32°C), very crowded, accommodation at maximum prices, Bellagio ferry queues can be 30+ minutes. October: beautiful autumn colour, some villas beginning to close, weather less predictable. November–February: most villas closed, reduced ferry schedule, authentic quiet, low prices.

**Î: What food should I eat at Lake Como?**
R: The lake's distinctive cuisine: missoltini (or misultitt in dialect) — dried and salted agone (shad) fish, a preservation tradition centuries old, grilled and served with polenta; risotto con filetti di pesce persico — creamy risotto with pan-fried perch fillets in browned butter and sage; lavarello al cartoccio — local whitefish baked in foil; polenta uncia — polenta enriched with Bitto cheese from the Valtellina; miascia — a traditional Como cake with bread, apples, raisins, and pine nuts. Key rule: the best lake fish is NOT at restaurants with the best lake views — those places pay premium real estate and often use frozen imported perch. Walk two streets back from the water.

**Î: Which villas can I visit on Lake Como?**
R: Main villas open to visitors in 2026: Villa del Balbianello (Lenno/Tremezzina): gardens €14, guided tour €25, open mid-March to end of December except Monday and Wednesday. Villa Carlotta (Tremezzo): botanical garden famous for spring azaleas and rhododendrons, plus sculpture collection. €15. Villa Monastero (Varenna): botanical garden along the lake shore for over 2 km, eastern shore alternative with far fewer crowds. €10. Villa Melzi (Bellagio): lakefront Japanese-inspired garden. €10. Villa Serbelloni gardens (Bellagio, owned by the Rockefeller Foundation): €15, advance booking recommended. George Clooney's Villa Oleandra (Laglio): not open to visitors, visible from the water.

---

## Layover vs Direct Flight 2026: When a Connection Saves Money and When It Does Not

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/zboruri/layover-vs-direct-flight
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** zboruri
**Publicat:** 2026-07-30
**Actualizat:** 2026-07-30
**Traducere a:** [zbor-cu-escala-vs-direct](https://plecari.com/ro/zboruri/zbor-cu-escala-vs-direct)

**Descriere:** Layover vs direct flight: real savings on European routes, the risks, reliable hub airports, how to protect yourself if you miss a connection, and turning a layover into a city visit.

**Rezumat rapid:** On short European routes (under 4 hours direct), direct flights almost always win — savings with a layover are typically €10–30, not enough to justify added time and connection risk. On intercontinental routes (USA, Asia, Africa), a layover can save €200–500 — a difference that justifies 3–5 extra hours of travel. The rules: same booking reference (single PNR) for protection, minimum 90 minutes for intra-EU connections or 2–3 hours for international, and reliable hubs (Istanbul, Vienna, Amsterdam, Dubai). With separate tickets you are on your own if you miss the connection.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: Is a connecting flight worth it to save money?**
R: On European routes under 4 hours direct: rarely. Savings are typically €10–30, not worth the added 2–4 hours and connection risk. On intercontinental routes of 8+ hours: often yes. Savings of €200–500 justify 3–5 extra travel hours. The formula: divide savings by hours added — if the result exceeds €40–50 per hour, the layover is rational.

**Î: What happens if I miss my connecting flight?**
R: If both flights are on a single booking (same PNR): the airline rebooks you on the next available flight at no charge, provides meals and accommodation if needed, and you may be owed EU261 compensation (€250–600) if you arrive 3+ hours late. With separate tickets: you buy a new ticket at the current price — potentially €500–1,500 for intercontinental routes.

**Î: What is the minimum recommended layover time?**
R: 90 minutes minimum for intra-EU connections at efficient hubs (Vienna, Amsterdam). 2 hours minimum for international connections. 3 hours minimum if you are changing airports (Heathrow to Gatwick, CDG to Orly). A 45-minute flight delay is common — you need genuine buffer, not just the minimum transfer time.

**Î: Are bags automatically transferred at a layover?**
R: Yes, if you have a single ticket (same PNR). Bags are checked through to the final destination — you do not collect them at the connection. With separate tickets, you must collect bags, clear customs and immigration, and re-check-in for the second flight — allow minimum 2–3 hours. Travelling with hand luggage only with separate tickets reduces this to 30–45 minutes.

**Î: Which airports are best for layovers?**
R: Most reliable: Istanbul IST (Turkish Airlines, modern and efficient), Vienna VIE (small, well-organised, Lufthansa Group), Dubai DXB (Emirates, excellent for Asia-Pacific). Solid: Amsterdam AMS, Frankfurt FRA. Problematic: London Heathrow LHR (consistently congested, high delay rates), Paris CDG (slow inter-terminal transfers).

**Î: What is an open-jaw itinerary?**
R: Open-jaw means flying into one city and returning from a different one — for example, flying to Rome and returning from Barcelona. You explore two destinations without retracing your route. The cost is typically similar to a standard return ticket on a single route. Search engines like Kiwi.com are designed to find these combinations automatically.

**Î: Is an 8-hour layover worth leaving the airport?**
R: Absolutely. Istanbul with 6 hours: Sultanahmet and the Grand Bazaar are 38 minutes by metro. Amsterdam with 5 hours: the canals and Jordaan are 15 minutes by train. Vienna with 6 hours: the Ringstrasse and a Viennese coffee at Café Sacher, 16 minutes by S-Bahn. Turkish Airlines and Emirates have official stopover programmes with included hotel packages.

**Î: Does travel insurance cover a missed connection?**
R: Only if the policy explicitly includes 'missed connection' or 'travel delay' coverage. This clause covers the cost of a new ticket if you miss a connection due to an unavoidable cause (delayed inbound flight). Check your policy wording before departure — this is the most important clause for travellers booking separate tickets on long-haul routes.

## London City Break from Bucharest 2026: Flights, Budget, Itinerary & Everything You Need

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/city-breaks/london-city-break-from-bucharest
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** city-breaks
**Publicat:** 2026-07-31
**Actualizat:** 2026-07-31
**Traducere a:** [city-break-londra-bucuresti-2026](https://plecari.com/ro/city-breaks/city-break-londra-bucuresti-2026)

**Descriere:** London city break from Bucharest 2026. Cheapest flights, transport from the airport, free museums, where to stay on a budget and what insurance you need post-Brexit.

**Rezumat rapid:** A London city break from Bucharest in 2026 costs €400–700 per person for 3–4 nights, including direct flights (from €50 one-way with Wizz Air to Luton), accommodation (€60–120/night), transport (£8.90/day Oyster or contactless), and meals. London has world-class free museums (British Museum, Natural History Museum, Tate Modern, V&A — all free), world-class theatre, and iconic neighbourhoods. Remember: the UK is post-Brexit, so you need a travel insurance with UK cover and an eSIM or UK data plan — your EU roaming doesn't apply.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: How much does a London city break from Bucharest cost in 2026?**
R: A realistic budget for 3 nights in London from Bucharest: flights €100–200 return (Wizz Air/Ryanair), accommodation €180–360 (3 nights at €60–120/night), transport £27 (3-day Oyster/contactless), food €150–250 (mix of markets, pubs, and one restaurant meal/day), attractions €50–100 (some are free). Total: €500–900 per person. Budget travellers can manage €400; those staying in zone 1 hotels and doing paid attractions will spend €700–1,000+.

**Î: Do I need a visa for London as a Romanian citizen?**
R: No, Romanian citizens do not need a visa for short stays in the UK as tourists (up to 6 months). The UK Electronic Travel Authorisation (ETA) introduced in 2024 is now required — it costs £10 and takes a few minutes to apply online. Apply at least 72 hours before travel. Without an ETA, you may be denied boarding.

**Î: Which airport for cheap flights from Bucharest to London?**
R: Wizz Air flies to London Luton (LTN) — the cheapest option but 35 km from central London (train or bus adds 45–60 minutes). Ryanair flies to Stansted (STN), similar distance. Tarom and others occasionally fly to Heathrow (LHR) or Gatwick (LGW) — more central but usually more expensive. For budget travel, Luton + the Luton Airport Parkway train (£12, 30 min to St Pancras) is the best combination.

**Î: Do I need travel insurance for London?**
R: Yes — and more than for EU destinations. Since Brexit, the UK is no longer part of EU reciprocal healthcare arrangements. The European Health Insurance Card (EHIC) is NOT valid in the UK. A single night of hospitalisation in a London NHS A&E can cost thousands without valid insurance. Travel insurance with UK cover is essential — it typically costs only €15–25 for a week.

**Î: Do I need an eSIM or UK SIM for London?**
R: Yes. Your Romanian SIM card does not benefit from free EU roaming in the UK (post-Brexit). Your carrier will charge €3–15 per day for data roaming. A UK eSIM from Airalo, Saily, or Yesim costs €5–12 for 7 days of data (3–10 GB) — roughly 80–90% cheaper than standard roaming. Install it before you fly: you activate it the moment you land at Heathrow or Luton.

**Î: What are the best free things to do in London?**
R: London has more world-class free attractions than any other city: British Museum (Egyptian mummies, Rosetta Stone, Elgin Marbles), Natural History Museum (dinosaur skeletons, blue whale skeleton), Victoria & Albert Museum (the world's greatest design museum), Tate Modern (contemporary art), National Gallery (Vermeer, Turner, van Gogh), Science Museum, National Portrait Gallery, and the Changing of the Guard at Buckingham Palace (free, check times). All free, all year.

**Î: Is London worth visiting for a 3-day city break?**
R: Absolutely. London rewards short visits precisely because so many world-class things are free. In 3 days you can cover the British Museum, Borough Market, Tower Bridge, a West End show, Camden Market, Notting Hill, and a Thames walk — all without feeling rushed. The city is extremely well-connected by the Underground and is very walkable between zones 1–2.

**Î: What's the cheapest way to get around London?**
R: Use your contactless bank card or phone directly on the Tube, buses, and Overground. TfL caps daily spending at £8.90 (zones 1–2, weekday) and £5.25 (zones 1–2, weekend) — unlimited travel within those zones. Never buy single paper tickets (they cost up to £7 per journey). Get an Oyster card only if you want a physical card — contactless is identical and works on arrival.

## Lost Luggage: Your Airline Rights and How to Claim Compensation in 2026

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/zboruri/lost-luggage-airline-rights
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** zboruri
**Publicat:** 2026-07-29
**Actualizat:** 2026-07-29
**Traducere a:** [bagaj-pierdut-companie-aeriana-drepturi](https://plecari.com/ro/zboruri/bagaj-pierdut-companie-aeriana-drepturi)

**Descriere:** What to do when your bag doesn't arrive, how much compensation you're entitled to under the Montreal Convention, what airlines must pay for delayed baggage, and when travel insurance fills the gaps.

**Rezumat rapid:** If your luggage doesn't appear on the belt, report it to the airline's Lost & Found desk before leaving the airport — you must complete a PIR (Property Irregularity Report) to establish your legal claim. 90% of 'lost' bags are actually delayed and recovered within 24–48 hours. Under the Montreal Convention, the maximum compensation for genuinely lost luggage is approximately €1,500–1,700 per passenger. Airlines must also reimburse 'necessary and reasonable' expenses incurred during a baggage delay — keep every receipt.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: What is the difference between delayed and lost luggage?**
R: Legally, luggage is 'delayed' (temporarily mishandled) for up to 21 days after the flight. It becomes officially 'lost' only after 21 days without being located. 90% of bags reported missing are actually delayed — they went on a different flight, were left at a connection airport, or were loaded incorrectly. The airline is obligated to locate and deliver them to your address, at their expense.

**Î: How much compensation do I get for lost luggage?**
R: The Montreal Convention caps airline liability at approximately 1,288 Special Drawing Rights (SDR), which translates to roughly €1,500–1,700 per passenger (the rate fluctuates with currency). This applies regardless of the actual value of the contents. If you carry high-value items, you can declare a higher value at check-in and pay a supplemental fee for increased coverage — otherwise the cap applies.

**Î: What expenses does the airline reimburse for delayed baggage?**
R: Necessary and reasonable expenses incurred because of the delay: essential clothing, toiletries, medication you need and couldn't bring in cabin baggage. The standard is 'necessary and reasonable' — not designer replacements. Keep all receipts. Airlines do not have a fixed daily allowance — they assess submitted receipts against the reasonableness standard.

**Î: What if my luggage arrives damaged?**
R: Report the damage to the airline's Lost & Found desk immediately — before leaving the airport. Photograph the damage thoroughly. Submit a written claim within 7 days of receiving the bag (not 7 days from the flight — 7 days from when the damaged bag was delivered to you). After 7 days without reporting, airlines typically reject damage claims.

**Î: Does travel insurance cover lost luggage better than the Montreal Convention?**
R: Often yes, in two ways: higher coverage limits (many policies cover €1,500–3,000 per person for lost bags, plus specific sub-limits for electronics and valuables), and faster, simpler claims processing through the insurer rather than the airline. The key difference: travel insurance pays you directly and quickly, then recovers from the airline if applicable. Airline claims can take months.

**Î: What should I never put in checked luggage?**
R: Valuables (jewellery, cash, expensive watches), electronics (laptops, cameras, tablets), prescription medication you need on the trip, passports and travel documents, keys to your home or car, and irreplaceable items. Airline liability for these items in checked baggage is limited — the Montreal Convention cap and the airline's general conditions typically exclude or significantly limit coverage for these categories.

**Î: Can I track my bag in real time?**
R: Most airlines now provide bag tracking through their app (Ryanair, easyJet, British Airways, Lufthansa, Turkish Airlines all have this). Apple AirTags and Tile trackers are allowed by IATA guidelines in checked baggage (set to Lost Mode) — they provide location data that can help locate a mishandled bag. Note: report AirTag presence to the airline if asked; regulations on tracking devices in luggage vary.

## Málaga and Costa del Sol 2026: The Complete Guide — Picasso, Caminito del Rey, Beaches & Real Budgets

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/city-breaks/malaga-complete-guide-2026
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** city-breaks
**Publicat:** 2026-08-04
**Actualizat:** 2026-08-04
**Traducere a:** [malaga-ghid-complet-2026](https://plecari.com/ro/city-breaks/malaga-ghid-complet-2026)

**Descriere:** The ultimate 2026 guide to Málaga and the Costa del Sol. How to skip lines at the Picasso Museum, secure Caminito del Rey tickets, real prices and neighborhoods.

**Rezumat rapid:** Málaga has transformed from a mere transit airport into Southern Spain's cultural powerhouse. In 2026, the recommended daily budget is €90–130 per person. Major attractions like the Picasso Museum (€12) and Caminito del Rey (€14) require booking months in advance. The ideal time to visit is May–June and September–October. From the airport, the Cercanías (C1) train brings you to the center in 12 minutes for just €1.80.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: Is Málaga worth visiting in 2026, or is it just a transit airport?**
R: Málaga has undergone a massive urban renaissance over the past decade. It is no longer just a gateway to Marbella's resorts, but one of Europe's most vibrant cultural hubs. Featuring over 30 museums (including the Pompidou Centre and the Picasso Museum), a revitalized port area (Muelle Uno), and a lively pedestrian historic center, Málaga deserves at least 2 to 3 days dedicated entirely to the city before exploring the rest of the coast.

**Î: How many days do you need for Málaga and the Costa del Sol?**
R: To truly experience the Andalusian rhythm, you need a minimum of 5 full days. Dedicate 2 days to Málaga city (Alcazaba, Picasso Museum, Soho), 1 day for the spectacular Caminito del Rey hike, and the remaining 2 days to explore the Costa del Sol beaches (such as Nerja to the east or Marbella to the west). A full week is the ideal scenario.

**Î: How do I get from Málaga Airport to the city center?**
R: The fastest, cheapest, and most efficient method in 2026 is the Cercanías commuter train (Line C1). The train station is located right outside Terminal 3 (Arrivals). Trains run every 20 minutes, the trip to the final station Málaga Centro-Alameda takes exactly 12 minutes, and a ticket costs just €1.80. The airport express bus (Line A) is also available, but it takes longer due to traffic.

**Î: Is the Caminito del Rey hike dangerous in 2026?**
R: Categorically not. Although it was dubbed 'the world's most dangerous path' in the 1990s, the trail was completely rebuilt from scratch and reopened in 2015. It now features wide wooden boardwalks, solid steel handrails, and safety nets. It is entirely safe for anyone with normal physical fitness. However, because the walkways are suspended 100 meters in the air, it is not recommended for those suffering from severe clinical vertigo.

**Î: When is the best time to visit Málaga?**
R: Spring (April through mid-June) and autumn (September through November) are absolutely ideal. Temperatures range between 22°C and 28°C, perfect for museums, hiking, and even beach days. Avoid July and August, when the region frequently faces extreme heatwaves (over 35°C) and the dry 'Terral' wind, and accommodation prices double.

**Î: What is an 'Espeto' in Málaga?**
R: Espeto is the soul of Málaga's local gastronomy. It consists of 6 to 7 fresh sardines skewered on a bamboo stick and grilled over an open fire (traditionally on olive wood placed inside old fishing boats filled with sand), right on the beach at small restaurants called 'chiringuitos'. An authentic espeto in the Pedregalejo neighborhood costs between €5 and €7.

## Marseille and Provence 2026: The Complete Guide — Vieux-Port, Calanques, Gastronomy & Real Budgets

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/city-breaks/marseille-complete-guide-2026
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** city-breaks
**Publicat:** 2026-08-05
**Actualizat:** 2026-08-05
**Traducere a:** [marsilia-ghid-complet-2026](https://plecari.com/ro/city-breaks/marsilia-ghid-complet-2026)

**Descriere:** The ultimate 2026 guide to Marseille and Provence. How to visit the Calanques National Park, the secret of authentic bouillabaisse, beaches, and real prices.

**Rezumat rapid:** Marseille is France's oldest city and the vibrant capital of the Provence region. In 2026, the recommended daily budget is €90–130 per person. Major attractions include the Vieux-Port, the Mucem museum (€11), and the stunning Calanques National Park. The ideal time to visit is May–June and September–October. From Marseille Provence Airport, the shuttle bus brings you to the central station in 30 minutes for €10.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: Is it worth visiting Marseille in 2026?**
R: Absolutely. Marseille has undergone a massive urban transformation, combining 2,600 years of history with an effervescent cultural scene. It is France's most cosmopolitan city, offering a unique gastronomy (the famous bouillabaisse), world-class modern architecture (Mucem), and direct access to some of Europe's most spectacular natural landscapes (Calanques National Park).

**Î: How many days do you need to visit Marseille?**
R: For a complete city break covering both the city and a day trip to Calanques National Park or the villages of Provence, you need a minimum of 4 full days. Dedicate 2 days to the historic neighborhoods (Le Panier, Vieux-Port, La Corniche) and museums, and the remaining days to nature and beaches.

**Î: How do I get from Marseille Provence Airport to the city center?**
R: The simplest method is the official shuttle bus which departs in front of the terminal every 10-15 minutes and takes you directly to the central St. Charles railway station. The trip takes about 30 minutes, and a ticket costs around €10. Alternatively, you can use a taxi or private transfer, but the cost is significantly higher.

**Î: Is Marseille safe for tourists in 2026?**
R: Yes, in areas frequented by tourists (Vieux-Port, Le Panier, Corniche, Mucem, main beaches), Marseille is as safe as any other major European city. As a general rule, avoid northern peripheral neighborhoods (quartiers nord) at night and remain vigilant in public transport or train stations against pickpockets.

**Î: What is the ideal period for a holiday in Marseille?**
R: Spring (May–June) and autumn (September–October) are the ideal seasons. Temperatures are mild (22–26°C), perfect for hiking in the Calanques and urban exploration, while summer crowds are reduced. July and August bring intense heatwaves and high accommodation prices.

**Î: What is Bouillabaisse and where can you eat it?**
R: Bouillabaisse is Marseille's iconic traditional fish soup, originally created by local fishermen. It contains at least 4-5 species of rock fish, cooked with saffron, fennel, and garlic, served with croutons and rouille sauce. It is a complex and expensive dish (between €50 and €90+ per person at certified restaurants following the official Bouillabaisse charter).

## Milan 2026: The Complete Guide — Duomo, Last Supper, Aperitivo & the City Beyond Fashion Week

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/city-breaks/milan-complete-guide-2026
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** city-breaks
**Publicat:** 2026-07-31
**Actualizat:** 2026-07-31

**Descriere:** Milan 2026 complete guide. Duomo, The Last Supper tickets, Navigli, fashion district, day trips to Lake Como and Cinque Terre, and real budget breakdown.

**Rezumat rapid:** Milan (Milano) is Italy's financial, fashion, and design capital — but beneath the designer boutiques lies a medieval city of extraordinary art. Must-sees: The Duomo (construction began 1386, finished 1965 — 579 years, 3,400 statues, rooftop walkable among 135 marble spires — €5 entry, €15 rooftop), Leonardo da Vinci's Last Supper at Santa Maria delle Grazie (15 minutes guaranteed, €17 + booking fee — books out 3–6 weeks ahead), and the Pinacoteca di Brera (Raphael, Caravaggio, Mantegna, established by Napoleon in 1809). 2026 special context: Milan co-hosted the Winter Olympics opening ceremony in February 2026 — the city has new infrastructure, regenerated neighbourhoods, and an international energy that's still present. Best time to visit: March–May and September–November.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: How do I book tickets for the Last Supper in Milan?**
R: The Last Supper (Il Cenacolo di Leonardo da Vinci) at Santa Maria delle Grazie is one of the hardest tickets in Italy to secure. Individual tickets (€17 + €3.50 booking fee) are released in blocks, usually 3 months ahead, at cenacolovinciano.vivaticket.com. In summer, these sell out within hours of release. If you can't get individual tickets: book a guided tour through GetYourGuide — tour operators hold a separate block allocation and often have availability when individual tickets are gone. You get 15 minutes inside the refectory, in groups of 25 maximum.

**Î: Is the Milan Duomo worth it and which ticket should I buy?**
R: Yes, absolutely. The cathedral itself (entry ~€5) is extraordinary — but the real experience is the Terrazza (rooftop), where you walk among 135 marble spires and 3,400 statues at rooftop level with the Alps visible on clear days. The rooftop can be reached by stairs or lift: stairs €5 extra, lift €8–13. A combined ticket (cathedral + rooftop + museum) costs approximately €18–22. The rooftop is open even in bad weather and is the highlight of the Duomo visit.

**Î: What is Michelangelo's Rondanini Pietà and where is it?**
R: The Rondanini Pietà is Michelangelo's final sculpture, left unfinished at his death in 1564. It shows Christ being lowered from the cross — unlike his earlier Pietàs (the Vatican and the Florentine), this one is almost abstract, the figures elongated and merged, the surface rough and unpolished. Scholars believe he was working on it until 6 days before his death at age 88. It's housed in Castello Sforzesco (Sforza Castle), in a dedicated room in the Museo d'Arte Antica. Entry to the castle museums: €10.

**Î: What is aperitivo in Milan and when does it happen?**
R: Aperitivo is Milan's pre-dinner drinking ritual — ordering a cocktail (Campari Negroni, Aperol Spritz, or house Negroni) for €7–12, which comes with a buffet of finger food, crostini, olives, cheeses, and hot bites included. No extra charge for the food. It happens daily from approximately 18:00 to 21:00. The Navigli canal district and Brera are the classic aperitivo neighbourhoods. This is how Milanese unwind — not a tourist gimmick but a genuine social institution.

**Î: What are the best neighbourhoods to visit in Milan?**
R: Brera: artistic heart, Pinacoteca di Brera, independent boutiques, the best daytime neighbourhood. Navigli: canal-side bars and restaurants, aperitivo culture, best evening neighbourhood. Isola: creative, gentrifying, street art, best authentic Milan neighbourhood away from tourists. Porta Nuova: futuristic skyscrapers (UniCredit Tower, Bosco Verticale), Piazza Gae Aulenti, interesting contrast. Ticinese: adjacent to Navigli, more local than the canal strip itself, good for lunch.

**Î: How is Milan different from Rome and Florence?**
R: Milan is a working city first, a tourist destination second. It has less concentrated Renaissance art than Florence, fewer ancient Roman ruins than Rome — but it compensates with a different quality: the world's greatest piece of Italian Renaissance painting (the Last Supper), Michelangelo's final sculpture, a Gothic cathedral 579 years in construction, and an urban lifestyle — aperitivo, design, fashion, aperitivo — that is the most genuinely Italian of any major city. It's also cheaper than Florence in restaurants and accommodation.

**Î: Is Milan worth visiting for just 2 days?**
R: Yes — 2 days is enough for the Last Supper (morning of day 1), Duomo with rooftop (afternoon day 1), Brera neighbourhood and Pinacoteca di Brera (morning day 2), Sforza Castle and Parco Sempione (afternoon day 2), and Navigli aperitivo (evening day 2). The city is compact — metro reaches everything quickly. Day 3 adds Lake Como (1h by train) or lake Maggiore.

## MSC vs Costa vs Norwegian 2026: Which Cruise Line Should You Choose?

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/croaziere/msc-vs-costa-vs-norwegian
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** croaziere
**Publicat:** 2026-07-29
**Actualizat:** 2026-07-29

**Descriere:** Detailed comparison of MSC, Costa and Norwegian cruise lines on price, food, cabins, entertainment and itineraries. Plus Royal Caribbean, Celebrity and Holland America — which one fits your holiday.

**Rezumat rapid:** MSC is the best choice for families (children under 12 sail free on most itineraries, competitive prices, new ships). Costa is ideal for couples who want a relaxed Italian style at the lowest price point. Norwegian is perfect for independent travellers who dislike fixed schedules — Freestyle Dining lets you eat whenever and wherever you want, but costs 30–50% more than MSC/Costa. All three operate extensively in the Mediterranean with embarkation from Italian ports accessible by direct flight from most of Europe.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: Which cruise line is cheapest — MSC, Costa or Norwegian?**
R: Costa is typically the lowest base price, starting from €369–499/person for 7 nights in the Mediterranean. MSC is comparable at €399–599. Norwegian is 30–50% more expensive than both at €599–899/person. However, Norwegian sometimes includes more in the base fare (drinks, Wi-Fi, speciality dining) through its 'Free at Sea' promotions, which narrows the gap.

**Î: Which cruise line has the best food?**
R: Norwegian wins on variety and quality — 15–20 dining venues per ship, with speciality restaurants that genuinely rival upscale land restaurants. MSC and Costa both have good Italian food at the included dining room, with buffets of consistent quality. Celebrity Cruises (not in this comparison) is considered the industry leader for food quality in the premium segment.

**Î: Which cruise line is best for families with children?**
R: MSC leads for families. Children under 12 sail free on most MSC itineraries — a saving of €800–1,200 for a family of four. MSC also has age-specific kids' clubs (3–17), waterparks, and Cirque du Soleil shows. Royal Caribbean is comparable on facilities but more expensive. Disney Cruise Line is the premium family option at roughly double the price.

**Î: What is Freestyle Dining and is it worth the extra cost on Norwegian?**
R: Freestyle Dining means no fixed dinner time and no assigned table — you eat at any of Norwegian's venues whenever you want. Traditional cruise lines have two fixed dinner sittings (typically 6 PM and 8:30 PM). If you dislike the structure of fixed dining, Norwegian's flexibility is worth the 30–50% price premium. If you don't mind fixed times, MSC or Costa deliver comparable food at significantly lower prices.

**Î: Do all three lines sail the Mediterranean?**
R: Yes. All three have extensive Mediterranean programmes from May through October, with embarkation options from Italian ports (Civitavecchia/Rome, Genoa, Savona, Bari, Ravenna), Barcelona, and Athens. MSC and Norwegian have the most diverse itinerary options; Costa focuses primarily on the western and eastern Mediterranean with Italian ports as its main hubs.

**Î: Can I book a cruise on these lines as a solo traveller?**
R: Yes, but the single supplement is significant. Cabins are priced for double occupancy — solo travellers typically pay 100% of the double occupancy rate (i.e. full price for two, even occupying the room alone). Norwegian has some studio cabins designed for solo travellers on select ships, priced without the supplement. MSC and Costa occasionally run solo supplement discounts.

**Î: Which line is easier to reach from Eastern Europe?**
R: MSC from Civitavecchia (Rome) is the most accessible: direct flights from Bucharest, Warsaw, Prague, Budapest, and most Eastern European capitals take 1.5–2.5 hours. Costa from Savona (via Milan) is equally accessible. Norwegian's main Mediterranean embarkation points (Rome, Barcelona) are similarly reachable. All three are better options for Eastern European travellers than North American cruise lines based in Miami or Galveston.
