## Naples 2026: The Complete Guide — Pizza, Museums, Neighbourhoods, Transport & Everything You Need to Know

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/city-breaks/naples-complete-guide-2026
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** city-breaks
**Publicat:** 2026-07-31
**Actualizat:** 2026-07-31
**Traducere a:** [napoli-ghid-complet-2026](https://plecari.com/ro/city-breaks/napoli-ghid-complet-2026)

**Descriere:** Naples 2026 complete guide. Best pizza, Pompeii and Vesuvius day trips, historic centre, real budget, safety tips and how to get there from Bucharest.

**Rezumat rapid:** Naples (Napoli) is Italy's most intense, authentic, and complex city — 2,800 years of layered civilisations, the world's most important Roman antiquities museum, the best espresso on the planet, and the place that invented pizza. The historic centre is UNESCO World Heritage since 1995. Best time to visit: April–June and September–October. Minimum 2 full days in the city plus 1 day for Pompeii. Not an easy city, but it rewards enormously.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: Is Naples worth visiting in 2026?**
R: Absolutely — with the right expectations. Naples is chaotic, loud, unpredictable, and extraordinary. It has the world's most important Roman antiquities museum (MANN), one of the most profoundly moving sculptures ever created (Sanmartino's Veiled Christ), pizza that people make pilgrimages for, a metro system with stations designed by world-class artists, and an entire Greco-Roman city under your feet. If you're prepared for intensity, Naples is revelatory. More authentic, cheaper, and less tourist-polished than Rome or Florence — and more alive than either.

**Î: How many days do you need in Naples?**
R: Minimum 2 full days for the city: Spaccanapoli, MANN Archaeological Museum, Cappella Sansevero, Quartieri Spagnoli, Castel dell'Ovo, pizza. Add one day for Pompeii or Herculaneum (45 minutes by Circumvesuviana train). Add another for the Amalfi Coast or Capri if you have time. 3-4 days is the ideal window.

**Î: Is Naples safe for tourists in 2026?**
R: Yes — with normal urban precautions. The main risk is pickpocketing, concentrated on the Circumvesuviana train to Pompeii, Via Toledo, and around the central railway station at night. Tourist neighbourhoods (Centro Storico, Chiaia, Quartieri Spagnoli, Vomero) are safe day and evening. The Camorra exists but does not interact with tourists — no visitor has been involved in organised crime activity in over a decade. Naples is safer than Barcelona for tourist-targeted theft.

**Î: Da Michele vs Sorbillo — which pizza?**
R: Da Michele (1870): Margherita and Marinara only, E6, communal marble tables, queue 30 min to 2 hours, absolute purism. Famous from Eat Pray Love. Sorbillo: 12 pizza types, organic flour dough, more options, similar queue, on livelier Via dei Tribunali. Both are extraordinary. If you can only choose one: Da Michele for the iconic experience; Sorbillo for those who want variety.

**Î: What is the Cappella Sansevero Veiled Christ?**
R: The Velato Cristo is a marble sculpture made in 1753 by Giuseppe Sanmartino in which the veil covering Christ's body appears to be transparent damp fabric, not stone. Antonio Canova stated he would have given all his work to have created it. Entry E10, advance booking mandatory at museosansevero.it — sells out weeks ahead in season.

**Î: What is Napoli Sotterranea?**
R: A network of tunnels and cisterns excavated in volcanic tufa beneath the historic centre over 2,400 years. Greeks quarried tufa for construction, Romans expanded for aqueducts, WWII transformed them into air-raid shelters for nearly 1 million Neapolitans. Guided tour E10, 90 minutes, descends 40 metres below street level.

**Î: How do you get from Naples airport to the city?**
R: Alibus shuttle: Capodichino Airport to Piazza Garibaldi plus Molo Beverello (ferries), E5, every 20 minutes, 20-30 minute journey. Official taxi: fixed fare E21 to city centre, E24 to waterfront — confirm the fixed rate before entering. No direct metro to airport in 2026 (extension under construction).

**Î: What food should you try in Naples beyond pizza?**
R: Sfogliatelle (shell-shaped pastry with ricotta and citrus, eat it hot), baba al rum (rum-soaked sponge, perfected in Naples in the 18th century), cuoppo (street food cone of fried squid and prawns), espresso napoletano (denser than elsewhere in Italy, E1 at the bar standing), polpo alla luciana (octopus with tomatoes and capers near Castel dell'Ovo).

## Online Booking Fraud 2026: How to Spot Fake Travel Sites, Avoid Scams & Recover Your Money

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/cazari/online-booking-fraud
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** cazari
**Publicat:** 2026-07-31
**Actualizat:** 2026-07-31
**Traducere a:** [fraude-rezervari-online-vacanta](https://plecari.com/ro/cazari/fraude-rezervari-online-vacanta)

**Descriere:** Holiday booking scams 2026: fake hotels, cloned sites, phantom rentals. How to spot fraud before you pay and what to do if you've already been scammed.

**Rezumat rapid:** The most common online travel booking frauds are: fake sites that clone Booking.com or Airbnb (different URL, identical appearance), too-good-to-be-true offers on social media, accommodation listings on Facebook Marketplace without contracts, and phishing emails asking you to 're-confirm' card details. Signs of a legitimate site: exact correct URL (booking.com, not booking-holidays.com), HTTPS, clear company registration details, card payment accepted, and verifiable reviews. If you've been defrauded, act immediately: call your bank for a chargeback (best within 24–72 hours), file a police report, and report the site to Google Safe Browsing.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: What are the most common online travel booking scams in 2026?**
R: The five most prevalent: 1) Fake sites cloning Booking.com, Airbnb, or major airlines with slightly different URLs. 2) Holiday accommodation scams on Facebook Marketplace — pay a deposit, property doesn't exist or is already occupied. 3) 'Seller-initiated' contact on Airbnb or Booking asking you to pay outside the platform. 4) Phishing emails posing as your airline or hotel asking to 're-confirm card details'. 5) Too-good-to-be-true last-minute offers via WhatsApp or Instagram DMs. All share the same core: they separate you from money before you can verify the service is real.

**Î: How do I check if a travel website is legitimate?**
R: Five checks: 1) URL exactly matches the official site (booking.com, not booking-holidays.com or b00king.com). 2) HTTPS padlock present (necessary but not sufficient — fake sites can have HTTPS too). 3) Company registration details visible (registered business name, address, phone number). 4) Card payment accepted — legitimate sites accept Visa/Mastercard; fraud sites often demand bank transfer or cryptocurrency. 5) Independent reviews on Trustpilot or Google — search '[site name] scam' or '[site name] reviews' before paying.

**Î: What is a chargeback and how do I get one?**
R: A chargeback is a reversal of a card payment initiated by your bank when you dispute a transaction for goods or services not received. If you paid by credit or debit card for a booking that didn't materialise (hotel doesn't exist, airline tickets are fake, accommodation already sold), you call your bank, explain the fraud, and they initiate a chargeback against the merchant. Time limit: typically 60–120 days from the transaction date. Credit cards have stronger chargeback rights than debit cards. Act within 72 hours for the best success rate.

**Î: Is Airbnb safe to use?**
R: Yes — if you book entirely through airbnb.com or the official app. Fraud occurs when a 'host' contacts you and asks you to pay outside the Airbnb platform (bank transfer, PayPal Friends) for a 'discount'. The moment you leave Airbnb's payment system, you lose all Airbnb buyer protection. Legitimate Airbnb hosts never ask you to pay outside the platform.

**Î: How do I know if a hotel deal on social media is real?**
R: Assume any social media accommodation offer requires verification before payment. Steps: search the property name + address on Google Maps (does it exist?), check if it's listed on Booking.com or TripAdvisor with genuine reviews, verify the phone number with a quick call, and never pay by bank transfer for an accommodation found via Facebook or Instagram. Legitimate properties are on multiple booking platforms.

**Î: What should I do if I've already paid a scam site?**
R: Act immediately in this order: 1) Call your bank and request a chargeback — the sooner, the better. 2) File a police report (many countries now have online cybercrime reporting). 3) Report the site to Google Safe Browsing (safebrowsing.google.com/safebrowsing/report_phish). 4) Report to your national consumer protection authority. The brutal truth: if you paid by bank transfer or cryptocurrency rather than card, recovery chances are below 5%. Card payment gives you chargeback rights; everything else doesn't.

**Î: Are comparison sites like Skyscanner or Kayak safe?**
R: Comparison sites (Skyscanner, Google Flights, Kayak) are safe — they aggregate prices but typically redirect you to the airline or an OTA (Online Travel Agent) for actual booking. The risk is in the OTA you're redirected to. Established OTAs (Expedia, Kiwi.com, Bravofly) are generally safe. Less-known OTAs in search results should be verified before payment — check Trustpilot and look for their full business details.

## Overtourism in Europe 2026: New Tourist Taxes, Visitor Limits & How to Travel Smarter

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/city-breaks/overtourism-europe-2026-tourist-taxes
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** city-breaks
**Publicat:** 2026-07-14
**Actualizat:** 2026-07-14
**Traducere a:** [supraturism-europa-2026-taxe-limite](https://plecari.com/ro/city-breaks/supraturism-europa-2026-taxe-limite)

**Descriere:** Venice charges €10 entry, Barcelona doubled its tourist tax, Dubrovnik caps visitors at 4,000. Every new fee mapped, plus 5 strategies to avoid crowds and save money.

**Rezumat rapid:** Europe's most popular destinations have introduced aggressive anti-overtourism measures in 2026. Venice charges €5-10 per day-tripper (with proposals for €30-50). Barcelona has nearly doubled its tourist tax. Amsterdam raised accommodation tax to 16% (heading to 21% by 2030). Dubrovnik limits the Old Town to 4,000 visitors simultaneously. Santorini restricts cruise ship passengers. Solutions: travel in shoulder season (May-June, Sept-Oct), check cruise ship schedules, book attraction tickets online, and consider alternative destinations.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: What tourist taxes will I pay in Europe in 2026?**
R: Major taxes: Venice — €5-10/day access fee (day-trippers only, with QR code registration), Barcelona — up to €6.75/night, Amsterdam — 16% on accommodation, Rome — €3.50-7/night, Paris — €1-5/night, Dubrovnik — €2/night + 4,000 person cap in Old Town. These are charged ON TOP of accommodation prices and often aren't shown on Booking.com.

**Î: How do I avoid crowds at Europe's popular destinations?**
R: Three strategies: 1) Travel in shoulder season (May-June, September-October). 2) Avoid cruise ship days (check the port authority schedule for Venice, Dubrovnik, Santorini). 3) Visit attractions at opening time (8:00-9:00 AM) or after 5:00 PM. Alternatively: choose alternative destinations (Valencia instead of Barcelona, Puglia instead of Tuscany, Naxos instead of Santorini).

## How to Pay Abroad Without Fees in 2026: Revolut, Wise, Cash and the DCC Trap

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/city-breaks/pay-abroad-no-fees
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** city-breaks
**Publicat:** 2026-07-29
**Actualizat:** 2026-07-29
**Traducere a:** [cum-platesti-strainatate-fara-comisioane](https://plecari.com/ro/city-breaks/cum-platesti-strainatate-fara-comisioane)

**Descriere:** The best payment methods for travel: when to use Revolut, when to use cash, how to avoid Dynamic Currency Conversion, and which ATMs to use to avoid skimming.

**Rezumat rapid:** The best setup for paying abroad: Revolut or Wise as your primary card (zero foreign exchange fees, interbank rate), your regular bank card as a backup, and €100–200 in local cash for markets, small restaurants and taxis. Always refuse Dynamic Currency Conversion (DCC) — when an ATM or card terminal offers to charge you 'in your home currency,' always choose local currency instead. DCC costs 3–8% more than your card's conversion rate. On a €1,000 holiday spend, that is €30–80 wasted.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: Is Revolut safe to use abroad?**
R: Yes. Revolut is regulated as an electronic money institution in the EU and UK. For travel spending, it is one of the best tools available — interbank rate conversion with no markup, instant notifications, instant card freeze if lost, and spending analytics. Be aware of the free plan's limits: free ATM withdrawals up to €200/month (2% fee after that), and a small weekend markup on some currencies.

**Î: What is Dynamic Currency Conversion (DCC) and why should I always refuse it?**
R: DCC occurs when a card terminal or ATM offers to convert your transaction into your home currency — 'so you know exactly what you're paying.' It sounds helpful but the exchange rate applied is 3–8% worse than your card's rate. Always choose 'pay in local currency' regardless of what the terminal says. Your card (especially Revolut or Wise) does the conversion at a far better rate.

**Î: How much cash should I take on holiday?**
R: For EU destinations (France, Spain, Italy, Greece): €100–150 for a week is sufficient if you pay by card at restaurants and hotels. For non-EU destinations with more cash-based economies (Turkey, Morocco, Southeast Asia): €200–400 equivalent in local currency. Always withdraw from local ATMs rather than exchanging at the airport — airport exchange rates are consistently 8–12% worse than ATM rates.

**Î: Which ATMs are safe to use abroad?**
R: ATMs located inside bank branches are the safest — card skimming devices are almost never fitted on ATMs inside a bank. Avoid standalone ATMs on tourist streets, in bars, or near major attractions. Always cover the keypad with your hand when entering your PIN. If the card slot feels loose or has anything attached over it, use a different machine.

**Î: Can I use my regular bank card abroad?**
R: Yes, your Visa or Mastercard bank card works in virtually every country. The cost: typically 1–3% foreign transaction fee plus a currency conversion fee of 1–2%, charged by your bank. On a €1,500 holiday, that adds €30–75 in fees. Revolut or Wise costs €0–5 for the same spending. The bank card is best kept as a backup rather than a primary payment method.

**Î: Does contactless payment work everywhere in Europe?**
R: Almost everywhere in Western and Northern Europe (UK, France, Germany, Netherlands, Scandinavia), contactless is universal. In Southern and Eastern Europe, smaller restaurants, markets, and local taxis may be cash-only. In Turkey, major tourist areas accept cards widely; bazaars and local transport are often cash. Keep €50–100 local currency for these situations.

**Î: What is the best way to get foreign currency before travelling?**
R: Do not exchange money before you travel — airport exchange bureaux at your departure airport and bank branches at home offer poor rates. The best rates consistently come from withdrawing local currency at ATMs at your destination, using Revolut or Wise (which hold or convert at interbank rates). If you must have cash before departure, order it online through a specialist currency provider (Wise, moneycorp) rather than walking into a bank or airport counter.

## Popular Flights from Bucharest 2026: Routes, Real Prices and When to Book

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/zboruri/popular-flights-from-bucharest
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** zboruri
**Publicat:** 2026-07-30
**Actualizat:** 2026-07-30
**Traducere a:** [zboruri-populare-din-bucuresti](https://plecari.com/ro/zboruri/zboruri-populare-din-bucuresti)

**Descriere:** Flights from Bucharest OTP in 2026: top 15 routes with verified prices, Wizz Air vs Ryanair vs TAROM comparison, best booking windows and how to avoid hidden costs.

**Rezumat rapid:** The most popular flights from Bucharest are to London, Rome, Istanbul, Barcelona, Paris, Amsterdam, Dublin and Athens. Average round-trip prices in mid-season: Rome €70–130, Istanbul €60–120, London €90–180, Barcelona €90–180. Cheapest booking window: 6–8 weeks before departure, Tuesday–Thursday flights, outside school holidays. Wizz Air has the most direct routes from Bucharest (60+), Ryanair has expanded rapidly since 2024 with 35+ new routes.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: What is the cheapest destination to fly to from Bucharest?**
R: Budapest and Rome are consistently the cheapest: tickets from €35–45 return with Wizz Air. Budapest benefits from the short flight time (1h20) and very low local prices. Rome and Bari compete for second place, especially in off-season. Istanbul is the cheapest non-EU destination (from €50 return).

**Î: Is Wizz Air or Ryanair cheaper from Bucharest?**
R: It depends on the route and date. Wizz Air has more direct destinations from Bucharest (60+ vs 35+) and typically wins on Eastern Europe and Balkan routes. Ryanair is more competitive on Rome Ciampino, Milan Bergamo, and London Stansted/Luton. Essential: always compare both on a search engine — never directly on airline websites, as they don't show each other's prices.

**Î: When is the cheapest time to fly from Bucharest?**
R: Cheapest months overall: November, January, February (excluding Christmas/New Year). Spring (March–May) and autumn (September–October) offer good prices combined with excellent weather at Mediterranean destinations. July–August are the most expensive, with sharp peaks during the Romanian school summer holiday.

**Î: How much does baggage cost on Wizz Air from Bucharest?**
R: Small hand luggage (40×30×20 cm): free on all tickets. Extended hand luggage (cabin bag, with WIZZ Priority): €6–15 added at booking. Hold baggage 20 kg: €20–45 per segment (cheaper added at booking, significantly more expensive at check-in). A ticket showing €40 with hold baggage return can cost €80–130 total — always compare the complete price, not the base fare.

**Î: Are there direct flights from Bucharest to the USA or Asia?**
R: No direct flights in 2026. All intercontinental routes require a connection. Best options: Turkish Airlines via Istanbul (IST or SAW) for Asia, Africa, and the Middle East; Lufthansa via Frankfurt for the USA and Asia; KLM via Amsterdam for North America; Emirates via Dubai for Asia-Pacific and Africa.

**Î: What EU261 compensation can I claim on flights from Bucharest?**
R: All flights departing from Bucharest Henri Coandă are covered by EU Regulation 261/2004, regardless of the airline. Compensation for delays of 3+ hours at the final destination: €250 (flights under 1,500 km), €400 (1,500–3,500 km), €600 (over 3,500 km). This applies to Wizz Air, Ryanair, and all carriers operating from Romanian airports.

**Î: Is it worth using Wizz Discount Club?**
R: Wizz Discount Club (approximately €30–40/year) provides discounts of €10–40 per ticket. It pays for itself after 2–3 flights if you take 3+ Wizz Air trips per year. Not worth it for occasional flyers. Activate from the app or website when purchasing a ticket.

## Portugal Holiday Guide 2026: Lisbon, Porto and the Algarve — Complete with Real Costs

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/city-breaks/portugal-holiday-guide-2026
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** city-breaks
**Publicat:** 2026-07-30
**Actualizat:** 2026-07-30
**Traducere a:** [vacanta-portugalia-2026-lisabona-porto-algarve](https://plecari.com/ro/city-breaks/vacanta-portugalia-2026-lisabona-porto-algarve)

**Descriere:** Portugal holiday guide 2026: Lisbon, Porto and the Algarve. Real budgets, a 10-day itinerary, best beaches, hidden sea caves and what nobody tells you before you go.

**Rezumat rapid:** Portugal is the best value destination in Western Europe in 2026. Daily budget: €55–80 (versus €90–120 for equivalent experiences in Spain or Italy). Lisbon: tram 28 through historic neighbourhoods, pastéis de nata at €1.20, Alfama and free viewpoints, Sintra 40 minutes away by train. Porto: Port wine cellars with tasting from €10, UNESCO Ribeira waterfront, Francesinha, the best grilled fish in Europe. The Algarve: golden limestone cliffs, Benagil Sea Cave, Praia da Marinha, Ponta da Piedade. Flights from most of Europe from €60–120. A rental car is essential for the Algarve.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: How many days do you need in Portugal?**
R: Minimum 5 days for Lisbon + Sintra + Porto. Ideally 10 days for the full experience: 3 days Lisbon + 1 day Sintra + 3 days Porto + 3 days Algarve. For a single long weekend: choose Lisbon OR Porto — not both in 3 days, the rush diminishes the experience of both.

**Î: Is Lisbon or Porto better?**
R: Lisbon: larger, more cosmopolitan, beach access 30 minutes by train (Cascais), more intense nightlife. Porto: smaller, more authentic, 20–30% cheaper, better food, Port wine cellars with Douro river views. If you can: do both — the high-speed train takes 2h30 and costs €25.

**Î: Is Portugal cheaper than Spain?**
R: Yes, significantly — especially Porto versus Barcelona or Madrid. Coffee: €0.80–1.20 (vs €2–3 in Spain). Full meal: €8–14 (vs €12–18). 3-star hotel: €50–90/night (vs €80–130). Daily budget in Porto: €45–65 vs €70–100 in Barcelona.

**Î: When is the best time to visit Portugal?**
R: May–June and September–October: excellent weather (22–28°C), minimal queues, reasonable prices. July–August: hot (28–35°C in the Algarve), crowded and slightly more expensive — but still below other Mediterranean destinations. Winter: Lisbon and Porto are pleasant (15–18°C), the Algarve becomes quiet and very affordable.

**Î: Do you need a rental car in Portugal?**
R: Depends on your itinerary. Lisbon: no — metro, tram and walking cover everything. Porto: no — metro and walking. Sintra: no — train from Rossio station (€4.70, 40 minutes). The Algarve: absolutely yes. The beaches are spread along 150 km of coastline with minimal public transport between them.

**Î: Is Portugal safe for tourists?**
R: Portugal consistently ranks in the top 5 safest countries in the world (Global Peace Index). The main risk: pickpocketing on tram 28 and in crowded areas of Alfama. Use a crossbody bag, keep your phone in a front pocket. Otherwise: relaxed, welcoming, no significant issues.

**Î: What should you eat in Portugal?**
R: Pastéis de nata (€1.20 at Pastéis de Belém or Manteigaria), Francesinha in Porto (beer sauce, melted cheese, layers of meat — €8–10), grilled fish at Matosinhos (€12–18), bacalhau à Brás (salt cod with eggs and crispy potatoes — €8–12), ginjinha cherry liqueur served in a chocolate cup (€1.50 at Rossio Square stands).

**Î: Do I need an eSIM or special insurance for Portugal?**
R: Portugal is in the EU — free roaming applies with any EU mobile plan, and the EHIC covers emergency treatment at public hospitals. No eSIM needed. A full travel insurance policy (€15/week) adds repatriation, cancellation and baggage cover — recommended but not as critical as for non-EU destinations like Turkey or the UK.

## Romania Road Trip 2026: Bucharest to Transylvania in 7 Days — Complete Itinerary

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/inchirieri-auto/romania-road-trip-transylvania
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** inchirieri-auto
**Publicat:** 2026-07-12
**Actualizat:** 2026-07-12
**Traducere a:** [road-trip-transilvania](https://plecari.com/ro/inchirieri-auto/road-trip-transilvania)

**Descriere:** The ultimate Romania road trip itinerary: 7 days from Bucharest through Transylvania and back. Castles, medieval towns, Carpathian mountains, fortified churches, and the best food in Eastern Europe.

**Rezumat rapid:** A 7-day Romania road trip from Bucharest through Transylvania covers roughly 1,200 km and costs €500-900 per person (car rental from €20/day, fuel €80-100 total, accommodation €30-60/night, food €15-25/day). The ideal route: Bucharest → Sinaia (Peleș Castle) → Brașov → Sighișoara → Sibiu → Transfăgărășan Highway → Bucharest. You'll see medieval towns, fairy-tale castles, Carpathian mountain passes, fortified Saxon churches, and eat some of the best traditional food in Europe — all for a fraction of what Western Europe costs.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: Is Romania good for a road trip?**
R: Romania is one of the best road trip countries in Europe. The roads are well-maintained on main routes, fuel is cheap (€1.40/litre), traffic outside Bucharest is light, and the scenery — Carpathian mountains, medieval villages, rolling hills — is spectacular. The country is large enough to feel like a real adventure but compact enough to cover in a week.

**Î: How much does it cost to rent a car in Romania?**
R: Car rental starts at €20-25/day for a small car (Dacia Sandero, VW Polo) from international companies at Bucharest airport. A week rental with full insurance (CDW + TP + Super CDW) costs €180-300 total. Manual transmission is cheaper than automatic. Book 4-6 weeks ahead for best prices.

**Î: Is the Transfăgărășan Highway really that good?**
R: Yes. Jeremy Clarkson called it 'the best road in the world' on Top Gear, and he wasn't exaggerating. It's a 90 km mountain road climbing to 2,042 metres with hairpin turns, glacial lakes, and views that make you pull over every 500 metres. It's only open June-October (weather dependent). Check road status before planning.

**Î: Is Romania safe for tourists?**
R: Very safe. Romania has lower crime rates than most Western European countries. Standard precautions apply in Bucharest (watch for pickpockets in Old Town, use ride-hailing apps instead of street taxis). Rural Romania is extremely safe and locals are famously hospitable.

**Î: Do I need an international driving permit?**
R: If you have a driving licence from an EU/EEA country, your regular licence works. US, UK, Canadian, and Australian licence holders should carry an International Driving Permit (IDP) alongside their regular licence, though in practice most car rental companies accept English-language licences.

## Saily eSIM Review 2026: How It Compares to Airalo and Yesim

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/esim-roaming/saily-esim-review
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** esim-roaming
**Publicat:** 2026-07-29
**Actualizat:** 2026-07-29
**Traducere a:** [saily-esim-comparatie](https://plecari.com/ro/esim-roaming/saily-esim-comparatie)

**Descriere:** Detailed Saily eSIM review: real prices, coverage, VPN feature, how it compares to Airalo and Yesim, and which one to choose for your destination.

**Rezumat rapid:** Saily is NordVPN's eSIM product — available in 150+ countries, with competitive prices and a basic built-in VPN for public Wi-Fi security. Compared to Airalo (the market leader with 200+ countries and maximum plan variety) and Yesim (strongest regional plans and unlimited data options), Saily occupies the middle ground: trustworthy brand, good European coverage, slightly simpler plan structure. For most travellers, the right choice depends on destination: compare all three before buying, since prices vary by country. All three must be purchased before arriving in Turkey, where provider websites are blocked.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: Is Saily eSIM legitimate and safe?**
R: Yes. Saily is developed by Nord Security (the company behind NordVPN), which has been operating since 2012 with tens of millions of subscribers globally. It is not a new or unknown startup — it benefits from Nord's established infrastructure, security expertise, and regulatory compliance across EU and UK markets. Data plans are provided through local network partners in each country.

**Î: Does Saily include a real VPN?**
R: Saily includes a basic VPN feature that encrypts your connection on public Wi-Fi networks (hotels, cafés, airports). It is not the full NordVPN product — it lacks some advanced features like Threat Protection, dedicated IP, and multi-hop servers. If you specifically need a full VPN, you need a separate NordVPN subscription. For travel purposes (securing public Wi-Fi), the Saily VPN layer is sufficient for most users.

**Î: Is Saily cheaper than Airalo?**
R: Varies by destination. For European plans (France, Germany, Italy, Spain), Saily is often marginally cheaper per gigabyte than Airalo equivalents. For more exotic destinations (Southeast Asia, Africa, Latin America), Airalo's larger network of local providers sometimes produces better prices. The honest answer: check both before buying for your specific destination — the difference is usually $1–3 for a standard week's plan.

**Î: Can I use Saily for multiple countries in one trip?**
R: Yes — Saily offers regional plans covering multiple countries simultaneously. The 'Europe' plan covers 39+ European countries under a single plan, eliminating the need to buy separately for each destination. If your trip spans France, Italy, and Croatia, one European plan covers all three. Regional plans are usually slightly more expensive per GB than country-specific ones but save time and hassle on multi-country trips.

**Î: Can I install Saily and Airalo on the same phone?**
R: Yes, if your phone supports multiple eSIM profiles (most modern phones do). You can install profiles from different providers for different destinations and activate them individually. Many frequent travellers maintain separate eSIM profiles for their regular destinations (Turkey, USA, UK) and activate the relevant one before each trip.

**Î: Does Saily work in Turkey?**
R: Yes — but you must purchase and install before arriving. Since 2025, Turkish authorities block access to eSIM provider websites (including Saily) from within Turkey. If you try to buy after landing in Istanbul or Antalya, the website will not load. Install the eSIM at home, and it activates automatically when you land in Turkey.

**Î: What phones support eSIM for Saily?**
R: Saily works on any eSIM-compatible phone: iPhone XS or newer, Samsung Galaxy S20 series and newer, Google Pixel 3 and newer, and most Android phones released from 2021 onwards. Check by dialing *#06# on your phone — if an EID number appears, your phone supports eSIM.

## Sicily 2026: The Complete Guide — Palermo, Etna, Taormina, Agrigento & Everything You Need to Know

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/city-breaks/sicily-complete-guide-2026
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** city-breaks
**Publicat:** 2026-07-31
**Actualizat:** 2026-07-31

**Descriere:** Sicily 2026 complete guide. Palermo vs Catania, Mount Etna, Valley of Temples, Taormina, real budget breakdown, when to go and how to get around by car.

**Rezumat rapid:** Sicily is the Mediterranean's largest island and one of the world's richest concentrations of history, food, and natural drama — 2,800 years of successive civilisations (Greeks, Romans, Arabs, Normans, Spanish) layered into a landscape dominated by Europe's largest active volcano. In 2026, Etna is active (summit cable car operating, guided hikes to ~2,850 m; check INGV daily status). Best bases: Palermo (west) and Catania/Taormina (east). A car is essential for anything beyond the main cities. Best time: April–June and September–October. July–August: beach holiday viable but archaeological sites punishingly hot (40°C+).

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: Do I need a car in Sicily?**
R: Yes, for anything beyond Palermo or Catania city limits. Public transport in Sicily is slow and infrequent outside the main cities. Without a car, you cannot visit the Valley of the Temples on your own schedule, reach most beaches, explore the rural interior, or visit the Baroque towns of the Val di Noto efficiently. Book a car online before arriving — on the spot in summer it tends to be expensive and sold out. Watch the insurance: the base rental price often excludes full cover. Pay extra for zero-excess cover or bring your own excess insurance.

**Î: Is Mount Etna safe to visit in 2026?**
R: Yes. Etna is one of the world's most monitored volcanoes and is accessible to visitors year-round. The volcano was active in early 2026 (flank eruption in Valle del Bove, January 2026; Northeast Crater reactivation December 2025; eruptive episode 5-6 July 2026 that briefly closed Catania airport). This is normal Etna behaviour. The cable car operates to 2,500 m; guided tours go to approximately 2,850–3,000 m depending on daily conditions. Summit treks above 2,800 m require a licensed guide. Check INGV (ingv.it) or etnaexplore.com the morning of your visit for current altitude limits.

**Î: How many days do you need in Sicily?**
R: At minimum: 5–7 days covers Palermo, Etna, and either Taormina or Agrigento. 10–14 days covers the whole island properly: Palermo, Monreale, Cefalù, Etna, Taormina, Siracusa and Ortigia, Noto, Agrigento, plus some beach time. Sicily is large (25,000 km² — comparable to Wales or Maryland) and distances are greater than they look on a map.

**Î: What is the best airport to fly into for Sicily?**
R: Catania Fontanarossa (CTA) for the east: Taormina 50 km, Etna 30 km, Siracusa 60 km. Palermo Falcone-Borsellino (PMO) for the west: Palermo city 35 km, Cefalù 70 km, Agrigento 130 km. For a full-island itinerary, fly into one and out of the other — eliminating backtracking entirely.

**Î: What is the best time to visit Sicily?**
R: April–June and September–October. May is arguably the best single month: wildflowers on the hillsides, temperatures 20–26°C, sea warm enough for brave swimmers, archaeological sites without summer heat exhaustion (40°C+), and accommodation prices 30–40% below peak. September: warmest sea (25–27°C), visible crowds reduction after mid-month, grape harvest on Etna slopes.

**Î: What is Palermo's Arab-Norman architecture?**
R: From 827 AD to 1072 AD, Sicily was ruled by Arab emirs who transformed Palermo into one of the most sophisticated cities in the Mediterranean world. When the Norman Roger II conquered Sicily in 1072, rather than erasing what the Arabs had built, he incorporated their craftsmen and their aesthetic — Byzantine mosaics, Arab geometric decoration, and Norman stone architecture — into a unique synthesis. The result: Cappella Palatina (Palatine Chapel), the Cathedral of Monreale, the Church of San Giovanni degli Eremiti, and the Church of La Martorana — buildings that exist nowhere else on Earth and were inscribed as UNESCO World Heritage in 2015.

**Î: What is the difference between arancini and arancine?**
R: A critical Sicilian linguistic battle: in Catania and eastern Sicily, the rice ball is 'arancino' (masculine, cone-shaped like the Etna volcano). In Palermo and western Sicily, it's 'arancina' (feminine, round like the orange it resembles — arancia). Ordering the wrong version in the wrong city is a guaranteed conversation starter. The rice ball itself: fried arborio rice encasing a filling of ragù (meat sauce) or butter and mozzarella, coated in breadcrumbs. €2–3 each.

---

## Ski Travel Insurance 2026: What Is Covered, What Is Not, and How to Choose

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/asigurari/ski-travel-insurance
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** asigurari
**Publicat:** 2026-07-30
**Actualizat:** 2026-07-30
**Traducere a:** [asigurare-schi-munte](https://plecari.com/ro/asigurari/asigurare-schi-munte)

**Descriere:** Complete guide to ski and winter sports travel insurance in 2026. Piste rescue costs, off-piste cover, equipment insurance, trip cancellation, and the clauses that catch skiers out every season.

**Rezumat rapid:** Standard travel insurance does NOT cover skiing — it must explicitly state 'winter sports' or 'ski cover' to be valid on the slopes. The most important coverage: piste rescue and mountain rescue (helicopter evacuation costs €3,000–15,000 in the Alps), emergency medical treatment for ski injuries (knee ligament surgery: €15,000–40,000), and piste closure cover. Off-piste skiing requires explicit endorsement — without it, any injury off a marked run invalidates the entire medical claim. Buy ski insurance before departure; purchasing on the mountain after an injury has occurred is not possible.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: Does standard travel insurance cover skiing?**
R: Almost never. Standard travel insurance treats skiing as a hazardous activity and excludes it from medical and accident coverage unless winter sports cover is explicitly added or the policy specifically states it includes skiing. Always verify before purchase — look for 'winter sports,' 'ski cover,' or 'hazardous activities including skiing' in the policy wording.

**Î: How much does mountain rescue cost in the Alps?**
R: Helicopter rescue in the French, Swiss, Austrian, and Italian Alps costs €3,000–15,000 depending on complexity, duration, and whether a doctor flies with the rescue team. In some Alpine countries (France, Austria), rescue costs are partially covered by the piste operator's levy (already included in your lift pass). In Switzerland, costs can be higher. Without insurance, rescue is billed to the individual — payable within 30 days in most cases.

**Î: Is off-piste skiing covered?**
R: Only with an explicit off-piste endorsement. Most ski insurance policies distinguish between on-piste (marked runs within the ski area boundary) and off-piste (unmarked terrain, backcountry). An injury sustained off-piste on a policy without off-piste cover invalidates the medical claim entirely. If you ski off-piste at any point, even briefly, confirm your policy explicitly covers it.

**Î: What is piste closure insurance and is it worth it?**
R: Piste closure insurance pays a daily cash benefit (typically €30–50/day) when the ski area closes due to insufficient snow, extreme weather, or other causes outside your control. It does NOT refund your lift pass or accommodation — it pays a fixed sum per day of closure. Worth considering for peak-season bookings in lower-altitude resorts susceptible to snow shortages.

**Î: Does ski insurance cover equipment theft?**
R: Only if the equipment cover is explicitly included. Most ski policies offer optional equipment cover for skis, boots, poles, and helmet up to a stated limit (typically €500–1,500). Equipment must be properly secured when not in use — left unattended on a ski rack outside a restaurant is often excluded. Hired equipment is usually covered differently from owned equipment.

**Î: Can I buy ski insurance after I arrive at the resort?**
R: No legitimate insurer will sell you ski insurance after you have already started skiing — the insurable risk has already materialised. Buy before departure. If you are already at the resort and realise you are not covered: stop skiing until you have purchased coverage, then purchase online for the remaining days. Some insurers exclude the first 24 hours after purchase for this reason.

**Î: What happens if I am injured and cannot return on my original flight?**
R: Ski insurance covers the cost of extending your accommodation and rebooking your flight if a medical situation prevents you from travelling on the original date. This requires a medical certificate from the treating doctor stating that you are not fit to travel. The insurer typically requires pre-authorisation before booking a new flight.

**Î: Does ski insurance cover ski lessons?**
R: Injury during ski school lessons is covered under standard ski insurance — lessons on marked runs with a qualified instructor are treated as normal on-piste skiing. The exception: any lesson conducted off-piste requires the off-piste endorsement.

---

## Solo Travel in Europe 2026: The Complete Guide to Safety, Budget & the Best Destinations

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/city-breaks/solo-travel-europe-2026
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** city-breaks
**Publicat:** 2026-07-16
**Actualizat:** 2026-07-16
**Traducere a:** [calatorii-solo-europa-2026](https://plecari.com/ro/city-breaks/calatorii-solo-europa-2026)

**Descriere:** Everything you need for your first (or tenth) solo trip through Europe. Safety, loneliness, budget, best cities for solo travellers, and the mindset shift that changes everything.

**Rezumat rapid:** Solo travel in Europe in 2026 is safe, affordable, and increasingly normal — 25%+ of European bookings are solo. Best cities for first-time solo travellers: Lisbon (warm, walkable, social hostel scene), Bucharest (ultra-cheap, great nightlife, easy English), Budapest (thermal baths, ruin bars, fellow solo travellers everywhere), Barcelona (beach + culture + tapas bar hopping), and Prague (compact, affordable, legendary beer culture). Budget: €45-90/day depending on destination. Safety: Europe is among the safest regions globally for solo travellers of all genders.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: Is solo travel in Europe safe?**
R: Yes. Europe is among the safest regions in the world for solo travellers of all genders. Standard precautions: use Bolt/Uber at night, keep phone and wallet in front pockets in crowded areas, share your itinerary with someone at home, and trust your instincts. The biggest risk isn't crime — it's overpaying for tourist traps.

**Î: How do I meet people while travelling solo?**
R: Stay in social hostels (common areas, bar, organised events), join walking tours and food tours (perfect for meeting other travellers), use apps like Meetup or Couchsurfing Hangouts, and sit at the bar (not a table) in restaurants and pubs. Solo travellers naturally gravitate toward each other — you'll make friends faster than you expect.

**Î: What's the cheapest way to travel solo in Europe?**
R: Hostels (€15-30/night), cooking simple meals or eating street food, walking instead of taxis, Interrail for multi-city trips, and travelling in shoulder season. A solo trip through Eastern Europe (Budapest, Bucharest, Belgrade, Prague) costs €40-55/day all-in.

## Hidden Fees in Car Rental: How to Avoid Paying Double

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/inchirieri-auto/taxe-ascunse-inchiriere-auto
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** inchirieri-auto
**Publicat:** 2026-07-09

**Descriere:** CDW, excess, fuel policy, airport surcharges, GPS fees — what awaits you at the counter and how to avoid every extra cost. A practical guide with real numbers.

**Rezumat rapid:** The most common hidden fees in car rental are: the excess on CDW insurance (you may pay €500–2,000 if you damage the car, even with basic insurance included), the airport surcharge (10–15% added when collecting from an airport), the young driver fee (under 25 years), overpriced GPS (€10–15/day) and the fuel policy trap ('full-to-empty' versus 'full-to-full'). You avoid them by reading the terms before booking and refusing add-ons at the collection counter.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: What is the CDW excess and why does it matter?**
R: CDW (Collision Damage Waiver) is the basic insurance included in the price, but it comes with an excess — the amount you pay out of pocket if you damage the car. The excess can be €500–2,000, blocked on your card as a deposit at collection. You can reduce the excess to zero with a third-party excess insurance (far cheaper than what the counter offers).

**Î: Is the extra insurance at the counter worth it?**
R: Almost never. Counter insurance costs €15–30 per day and is the rental industry's biggest upsell. A third-party excess waiver from a specialist (e.g. insurance4carhire, iCarhireinsurance, RentalCover) costs 3–5 times less for the same cover and the same period.

**Î: What is the 'full-to-full' fuel policy?**
R: You collect the car with a full tank and return it full. It is the fairest option — you pay only for what you use, at petrol station prices. The alternative 'pre-purchase fuel' means you pay for a full tank at collection (at the company's price, higher than a petrol station) and return the car empty — but you never manage to empty it exactly, so you always lose paid fuel.

**Î: Why is collecting at the airport more expensive?**
R: Airports charge rental companies a concession fee for access to the terminal, parking and counter space. Companies pass this cost directly to you — as an 'airport surcharge' of 10–15% added to the total. Collecting from a city-centre location avoids the surcharge, but you need to get there from the airport.

**Î: What does a one-way fee mean?**
R: A one-way fee applies when you collect the car in one city and return it in another. It can be anywhere from €30 to over €100, depending on the company and distance. Some companies include one-way within the same country for free — check at booking, not at the counter.

**Î: Can I use my credit card insurance instead of buying CDW cover?**
R: Some premium credit cards (Visa Signature, Mastercard World Elite, Amex Gold) include car rental insurance as a benefit. However, you typically need to pay the full rental on that card, decline the rental company's CDW, and the cover is secondary (it kicks in after other insurance). Check your card's terms carefully — exclusions vary and not all rental companies accept card insurance.

---

## Things to Do in Amsterdam 2026: Canals, Museums, Coffee Shops & Local Secrets

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/experiente/things-to-do-amsterdam
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** experiente
**Publicat:** 2026-07-25
**Actualizat:** 2026-07-25
**Traducere a:** [ce-sa-faci-in-amsterdam](https://plecari.com/ro/experiente/ce-sa-faci-in-amsterdam)

**Descriere:** Complete Amsterdam guide for 2026. Rijksmuseum, Anne Frank House, canal boats, coffee shops, cycling, and how to avoid the 16% tourist tax surprise.

**Rezumat rapid:** Amsterdam essentials: Rijksmuseum (€22, Rembrandt's Night Watch), Anne Frank House (€16, book 6–8 weeks ahead — it always sells out), Van Gogh Museum (€22), canal boat tour (€15–20), Jordaan neighbourhood (free, the most beautiful in the city), and a rented bicycle (€12/day). Daily budget: €80–120 — Amsterdam is expensive but worth it. Key warning: the tourist tax is 16% of your room rate and is NOT included in the Booking.com price shown.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: How many days do you need in Amsterdam?**
R: 2–3 days covers the essentials: Rijksmuseum, Van Gogh Museum, Anne Frank House, a canal boat, and Jordaan. 4–5 days lets you add NDSM Wharf, Zaanse Schans windmills, Keukenhof (spring only), and deeper neighbourhood exploration. A long weekend works if you prioritise ruthlessly.

**Î: Is Amsterdam expensive?**
R: Yes, one of Europe's pricier cities. Beer at a bar: €5–6. A sit-down meal: €18–30. 3-star hotel: €120–200/night PLUS the 16% tourist tax. Daily budget: €80–120. Money-saving tricks: eat at Albert Heijn supermarket, get the I Amsterdam City Card (€65/24h, includes transport + museums), and avoid restaurants on Damrak and Leidseplein.

**Î: Are coffee shops legal in Amsterdam?**
R: Cannabis consumption is tolerated (not strictly legal — an important Dutch legal distinction) in licensed coffee shops. Rules: maximum 5g per person, consumption inside only, no mixing with alcohol (most coffee shops don't serve alcohol anyway), and you must be 18+. Smoking outdoors in most central areas has been restricted since 2023. Possession on the street remains technically illegal.

**Î: Do I need to book Anne Frank House in advance?**
R: Yes, absolutely, and as early as possible — 6–8 weeks ahead minimum in summer. The Anne Frank House sells out completely and there are no walk-up tickets. Book directly on annefrank.org. Tickets: €16 adults, €7 children (10–17), free under 10.

**Î: What is the tourist tax in Amsterdam?**
R: Amsterdam charges 16% of the room rate as a tourist tax — the highest in Europe. On a €150/night hotel for 3 nights, that's €72 extra. This is charged at check-in and is not visible in the Booking.com or Airbnb listed price. Always factor it into your accommodation budget.

**Î: Is Amsterdam safe?**
R: Yes, it is one of Europe's safest capitals. The main risks are: bicycle theft (always use a good lock), pickpockets in crowded tourist areas (Damrak, Central Station), and traffic — cyclists have absolute right of way and will not stop for pedestrians. Stay aware on bike lanes, which look like pavements but aren't.

**Î: What is the best way to get around Amsterdam?**
R: Bicycle. The city is completely flat, has 800km of dedicated bike lanes, and cycling is how locals actually move. Rent from MacBike or Donkey Republic (€12–15/day). Alternatively: trams (€4/single, GVB day pass €9.50), ferries (free across the IJ river), and walking for the centre. Avoid cars — parking is €7.50/hour in the centre and the streets are narrow.

---

## Things to Do in Athens 2026: Acropolis, Neighbourhoods, Island Day Trips & Real Costs

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/experiente/things-to-do-athens
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** experiente
**Publicat:** 2026-07-15
**Actualizat:** 2026-07-15
**Traducere a:** [ce-sa-faci-in-atena](https://plecari.com/ro/experiente/ce-sa-faci-in-atena)

**Descriere:** Complete Athens guide for 2026. Acropolis tips, best neighbourhoods, street food, island day trips, transport, and why Athens is Europe's most underrated capital.

**Rezumat rapid:** Athens essentials: Acropolis (€20 or €30 combined ticket for 7 sites, go at 8 AM), Plaka (historic neighbourhood, free), National Archaeological Museum (€12, world-class), Monastiraki flea market (free), and a day trip to Hydra or Aegina by ferry (€30-60 return, 1 hour). Budget: €50-75/day. Gyro: €3-4. Metro: €1.20. Rooftop cocktail with Acropolis view: €10-12. Best months: April-June and September-October.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: How many days do you need in Athens?**
R: 2-3 days for the city itself. Add 1 day for an island trip (Hydra, Aegina, or Poros — all under 2 hours by ferry). If you're combining with the Greek Islands, 2 days in Athens + ferry/flight to the islands is perfect.

**Î: Is the Acropolis worth visiting?**
R: Absolutely — it's the single most important archaeological site in Western civilisation. But timing matters: go at 8:00 AM opening (before tour groups arrive), wear comfortable shoes (marble is slippery), bring water and a hat (zero shade), and book the €30 combined ticket which includes 6 other sites.

**Î: Is Athens safe?**
R: Yes. Athens is generally safe for tourists. Standard precautions: watch for pickpockets around Monastiraki and on the metro, avoid Omonia Square late at night, and use Bolt/Uber instead of unlicensed taxis.

## Things to Do in Barcelona 2026: Gaudí, Beaches, Gothic Quarter & Local Secrets

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/experiente/things-to-do-barcelona
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** experiente
**Publicat:** 2026-07-15
**Actualizat:** 2026-07-15

**Descriere:** Complete Barcelona guide for 2026. Sagrada Familia, Park Güell, Gothic Quarter, Barceloneta beach, tapas, and how to avoid the tourist tax surprise.

**Rezumat rapid:** Barcelona must-dos: Sagrada Familia (€26, book 3-4 weeks ahead — it WILL sell out), Park Güell (€10 timed entry), Gothic Quarter (free, get lost on purpose), Barceloneta beach (free, metro L4), La Boquería market (free entry, eat everything), and a rooftop drink at sunset. Budget: €65-100/day. Tourist tax: up to €6.75/night ON TOP of hotel price. Best months: May-June and September-October — summer is 35°C+ and extremely crowded.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: How many days do you need in Barcelona?**
R: 3-4 days is ideal. Day 1: Sagrada Familia + Eixample. Day 2: Gothic Quarter + El Born + Barceloneta. Day 3: Park Güell + Gràcia neighbourhood. Day 4: day trip to Montserrat or Costa Brava. A weekend (2 days) works if you prioritise Sagrada Familia + Gothic Quarter.

**Î: Do I need to book Sagrada Familia tickets in advance?**
R: Yes, absolutely. Sagrada Familia sells out 3-4 weeks ahead in summer. Without advance tickets, you cannot enter — there's no walk-up option. Book on GetYourGuide (free cancellation) or the official basilica website. €26 standard, €36 with tower access.

**Î: What is Barcelona's tourist tax in 2026?**
R: Barcelona has Europe's highest tourist tax: up to €6.75/night at 5-star hotels (regional + municipal combined). For a 3-night stay at a 4-star: €12-20 extra, charged at check-in and NOT shown on Booking.com. Full details in our overtourism guide.

## Things to Do in Berlin: Complete 2026 Guide with Prices, the Wall, Free Museums & Tips

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/experiente/things-to-do-berlin
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** experiente
**Publicat:** 2026-08-06
**Actualizat:** 2026-08-06
**Traducere a:** [ce-sa-faci-in-berlin](https://plecari.com/ro/experiente/ce-sa-faci-in-berlin)

**Descriere:** Complete Berlin 2026 guide — Brandenburg Gate, Reichstag dome, Holocaust Memorial, East Side Gallery, Checkpoint Charlie, Topography of Terror, Museum Island, Berghain, Potsdam day trip.

**Rezumat rapid:** Berlin deserves 4–5 days. Top priorities: Brandenburg Gate (free), Reichstag glass dome (free, advance online booking required), Holocaust Memorial (free), East Side Gallery (free), Topography of Terror (free), Museum Island (€14–22/museum). Currywurst: €4–5.50. Döner: €6–8. Berlin is cheaper than London or Paris, with dozens of major historical attractions completely free.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: Is Berlin expensive?**
R: Berlin is one of the most accessible major capitals in Western Europe. Currywurst: €4–5.50. Döner kebab: €6–8. Mittagstisch (weekday lunch special): €10–14. Dozens of major historical attractions are completely free. 3-star hotel: €80–140/night. Realistic daily budget: €80–120/person comfortably. Significantly cheaper than London, Paris, or Zürich.

**Î: Do I need to book the Reichstag in advance?**
R: Yes, mandatory. The Reichstag glass dome is free but must be booked online at bundestag.de at least 2–3 weeks ahead (sometimes more in summer). The booking requires passport or ID details for all group members. Without a reservation you cannot enter — no matter how long you queue.

**Î: What is a Späti and why does it matter?**
R: Späti (Spätverkauf = late-night shop) is Berlin's neighbourhood convenience store open late or 24 hours — beer, drinks, snacks, cigarettes. Beer price at a Späti: €1–2 versus €4–6 at a bar. Locals pre-drink at the Späti before going out — it's a completely accepted cultural practice and part of the city's identity.

**Î: Is Museum Island worth doing in full?**
R: If you have 2–3 days, choose selectively. Pergamonmuseum (partial renovation in 2026 — check smb.museum for open sections), Neues Museum (Nefertiti bust), and Alte Nationalgalerie (19th-century German art) are the most powerful. Combined ticket for all 5 museums: ~€18–22.

**Î: How do I get into Berghain?**
R: Berghain is the world's most famous club and has one of the most selective doors. There is no guaranteed formula. What works better: come alone or in a very small group (2–3 people), don't dress in standard clubwear, don't photograph the queue, don't talk much at the door, be patient. €25+ entry if you get in. If you don't (it happens), don't take it personally — the door is the club's policy, not a verdict on you.

---

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/experiente/things-to-do-bucharest

**Descriere:** The best experiences in Bucharest for 2026. Palace of Parliament, Old Town nightlife, food tours, communist history, street art, and day trips to Transylvania.

**Rezumat rapid:** Best Bucharest experiences: Palace of Parliament tour (€10-15, world's heaviest building), communist history walking tour (€15-25), Old Town food crawl (mici, sarmale, papanași — full meal €10-15), Therme Bucharest (€25, 30,000 m² of thermal pools), street art tour in Izvor/Uranus, and a day trip to Peleș Castle in Transylvania (90 min by train). Budget: €40-60/day. Beer: €2.50. Cocktail: €5-7. Uber across the city: €3-4.

For nightlife: the Old Town has 120+ bars within walking distance.

**Î: Is Bucharest worth visiting for more than a stopover?**

**Î: Is Bucharest safe?**
R: Yes, very safe for tourists. Lower crime rates than most Western European capitals. Use Bolt/Uber instead of street taxis, watch for pickpockets in the Old Town on weekend nights, and you'll have zero problems.

## Things to Do in Budapest 2026: Thermal Baths, Ruin Bars, Parliament & the Danube

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/experiente/things-to-do-budapest
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** experiente
**Publicat:** 2026-07-15
**Actualizat:** 2026-07-15
**Traducere a:** [ce-sa-faci-in-budapesta](https://plecari.com/ro/experiente/ce-sa-faci-in-budapesta)

**Descriere:** Complete Budapest guide for 2026. Széchenyi baths, ruin bars, Parliament tour, Fisherman's Bastion, best food, and why Budapest is Europe's best-value capital.

**Rezumat rapid:** Budapest highlights: Széchenyi Thermal Baths (€25, outdoor pools + slides), Parliament building (€12 guided tour), Fisherman's Bastion (free area, €4 tower), ruin bars (Szimpla Kert — beer €2.50-3.50), Danube night cruise (€10-20), and the Central Market Hall (free entry). Budget: €45-70/day — one of Europe's cheapest capitals. Goulash soup: €4. Craft beer: €3. Full restaurant meal: €10-15. Metro: €1.50.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: How many days do you need in Budapest?**
R: 2-3 days covers the essentials (baths, Parliament, Castle District, ruin bars, Danube cruise). 4 days lets you add Margaret Island, the Cave Church, Heroes' Square, and a deeper food exploration. Even 1 full day is rewarding if you prioritise baths + Parliament + ruin bar evening.

**Î: Which thermal bath is best in Budapest?**
R: Széchenyi for the classic experience (largest medicinal bath in Europe, outdoor pools, slides). Rudas for atmosphere (Ottoman-era, rooftop pool with panoramic views). Gellért for Art Nouveau elegance (beautiful interior but most expensive). Király for authentic Ottoman intimacy (smallest, least touristy).

**Î: Is Budapest cheap?**
R: Very. A full restaurant meal: €10-15. Craft beer at a ruin bar: €2.50-3.50. Széchenyi entry: €25. Metro: €1.50. A day in Budapest costs €45-70 — roughly half of what London, Paris, or Amsterdam costs. It's consistently ranked among Europe's best-value capitals.

## Things to Do in Dresden: Complete 2026 Guide with Prices, History & Insider Tips

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/experiente/things-to-do-dresden
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** experiente
**Publicat:** 2026-08-06
**Actualizat:** 2026-08-06
**Traducere a:** [ce-sa-faci-in-dresda](https://plecari.com/ro/experiente/ce-sa-faci-in-dresda)

**Descriere:** Complete Dresden 2026 guide — Zwinger Palace, Frauenkirche rebuilt from rubble, Semperoper, Sistine Madonna, Saxon Switzerland day trip. The full story of the 1945 bombing and the reconstruction.

**Rezumat rapid:** Dresden deserves 2–3 days. Top priorities: Zwinger Palace courtyard (free) and Old Masters Gallery with Raphael's Sistine Madonna (~€14), Frauenkirche rebuilt from original stones (nave free, dome €10), Semperoper guided tour (€14) or opera performance, and the Saxon Switzerland day trip (30 min by train). Dresden is cheaper than Munich or Berlin, with a reconstruction story that exists nowhere else in Europe.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: Why is Dresden called the 'Florence of the Elbe'?**
R: Dresden earned the nickname in the 18th century due to the Italian Baroque and Rococo architecture commissioned by Augustus the Strong — the Zwinger, Semperoper, Royal Palace, and Frauenkirche formed an architectural ensemble comparable to the finest in Europe. The historical irony: this very beauty attracted Allied attention in 1945, when Dresden was one of the few major German cities not yet bombed. It was attacked three months before the war ended.

**Î: What actually happened on the night of February 13, 1945?**
R: February 13–15, 1945: RAF (British) and USAAF (American) aircraft dropped over 3,900 tons of incendiary and high-explosive bombs on Dresden. The resulting firestorms reached 1,500°C and destroyed 1,600 acres of the city center. Approximately 25,000 people died, mostly civilians. The Frauenkirche collapsed the following morning. The debate about the military necessity of the attack continues — Dresden was not a major military target and the war was effectively already won.

**Î: How was the Frauenkirche rebuilt?**
R: The ruins stood in the city center throughout the Cold War as a deliberate memorial (an East German political decision). After reunification, reconstruction began in 1994, brick by brick, with original stones catalogued and reintegrated wherever possible. The dark, scorched stones are deliberately visible in the facade alongside lighter new sandstone — not a construction error, but an intentional design decision: a map of survival and renewal simultaneously. The reconsecration was held on October 30, 2005.

**Î: Is Dresden worth visiting compared to Berlin?**
R: They are different experiences. Berlin is the capital with Wall history, enormous free museums, and one of the world's best cultural scenes — it needs 4–5 days. Dresden is smaller, more Baroque, more intimate, with a unique reconstruction story and Saxon Switzerland 30 minutes away. 2 days are enough for Dresden, and it combines well with Berlin on a longer city break.

**Î: How do I get from Bucharest to Dresden?**
R: No direct flight. Most efficient: fly to Berlin (BER, 2h30 direct with Wizz Air) + train Berlin–Dresden (2h, €25–40). Or fly to Prague (2h direct) + train Prague–Dresden (2h15, €20–35). Alternatively, fly to Frankfurt or Munich + ICE train to Dresden (3–4h).

---

## Things to Do in Gdańsk: Complete 2026 Guide with Prices, Amber, Solidarity & Insider Tips

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/experiente/things-to-do-gdansk
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** experiente
**Publicat:** 2026-08-05
**Actualizat:** 2026-08-05
**Traducere a:** [ce-sa-faci-in-gdansk](https://plecari.com/ro/experiente/ce-sa-faci-in-gdansk)

**Descriere:** Complete Gdańsk 2026 guide — Old Town, WWII Museum, European Solidarity Centre, Malbork Castle, amber on Mariacka Street, Sopot beach, Tricity day trips. The Baltic port where history changed Europe.

**Rezumat rapid:** Gdańsk deserves 3–4 days. Top priorities: Długi Targ and Old Town (free), Museum of the Second World War (~€8, free Tuesdays), European Solidarity Centre (~€8), amber shopping on Mariacka Street, day trip to Malbork Castle (45 min by train, world's largest Gothic castle). Sopot is 15 minutes by train with Europe's longest pier. Polish prices — pierogi €5–7, craft beer €2–3, 3-star hotel €40–70/night.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: Why is Gdańsk historically significant?**
R: Gdańsk is where World War II began (September 1, 1939, the attack on Westerplatte) and where Communism began to unravel — in August 1980, Lech Wałęsa organized the strike at the Lenin Shipyard that created Solidarność, the first independent trade union in the Soviet bloc. This triggered the chain reaction that brought down Communist governments across Eastern Europe. The city's Hanseatic merchant architecture looks more like Amsterdam than Warsaw.

**Î: What is the amber from Gdańsk?**
R: The Polish Baltic coast produces 70–90% of the world's amber — fossilized tree resin 44 million years old, sometimes with perfectly preserved insects or plants inside. Gdańsk has been the center of the amber trade for at least 3,000 years. Mariacka Street is the commercial hub: jewelry, sculptures, and souvenirs, all in authentic amber. Buy from shops with certificates of authenticity, not from street stalls.

**Î: Is Malbork Castle worth the day trip?**
R: Absolutely. Malbork Castle (45 minutes by train from Gdańsk, ~€2 return) is the largest castle in the world by area and the most impressive Gothic castle complex in Central Europe — built by the Teutonic Knights from red brick in the 13th–15th centuries, UNESCO since 1997. Entry ~€25. Allow 3–4 hours. One of the most impressive day trips from any Central European city break.

**Î: What is Tricity (Trójmiasto)?**
R: Trójmiasto is the urban agglomeration of Gdańsk + Sopot + Gdynia. The SKM commuter train connects all three in 30–40 minutes total, with tickets at €1–2 per segment. Sopot is the resort town with Europe's longest wooden pier (511m), Monte Cassino (Poland's most animated pedestrian boulevard), and fine sandy beaches. Gdynia is a modern port city with an interesting naval museum. You can see all three in a single day.

**Î: When is the best time to visit Gdańsk?**
R: May–September: good weather, Sopot beaches open, cultural festivals. July–August: most animated, St. Dominic's Fair (Poland's oldest market, 750+ years). December: Christmas markets considered among Poland's most beautiful. Winter (Jan–Feb): minimum prices, quiet, but genuine Baltic cold (−5 to 5°C).

---

## Things to Do in Istanbul 2026: Hagia Sophia, Grand Bazaar, Bosphorus & Beyond

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/experiente/things-to-do-istanbul
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** experiente
**Publicat:** 2026-07-15
**Actualizat:** 2026-07-15
**Traducere a:** [ce-sa-faci-in-istanbul](https://plecari.com/ro/experiente/ce-sa-faci-in-istanbul)

**Descriere:** Complete Istanbul guide for 2026. Two continents, 2,500 years of history, the best street food in the Mediterranean, and why Istanbul might be the most fascinating city on Earth.

**Rezumat rapid:** Istanbul must-dos: Hagia Sophia (free, arrive at 8 AM), Blue Mosque (free, closed during prayer times), Topkapi Palace (€20 or Museum Pass), Grand Bazaar (free entry, 4,000+ shops), Bosphorus cruise (public ferry €2 or dinner cruise €40-60), and street food in Kadıköy. Budget: €40-65/day — incredibly affordable. Kebab meal: €5-8. Tea: €0.50. Ferry: €1. Museum Pass Istanbul: €55 (5 days, 12 museums). Non-EU visitors need an eSIM — roaming is expensive.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: How many days do you need in Istanbul?**
R: 3-4 days for the highlights (Sultanahmet, Grand Bazaar, Bosphorus, Kadıköy). 5-7 days to explore Balat, Karaköy, Prince's Islands, and the food scene properly. Even a long weekend (2 days) works if you focus on Sultanahmet + Bosphorus + Grand Bazaar.

**Î: Is Istanbul safe for tourists?**
R: Yes, Istanbul is very safe for tourists. Crime rates targeting visitors are low. Standard precautions: be wary of overly friendly strangers who invite you to their bar (the bill scam — see our scam guide), use Bolt for transport, and watch for pickpockets at the Grand Bazaar. The tourist police are responsive and helpful.

**Î: Do I need a visa for Istanbul?**
R: Most nationalities (US, UK, EU, Canada, Australia) can enter Turkey visa-free for up to 90 days. Passport must be valid for 6 months from entry date. National ID cards are NOT accepted.

**Î: Does my phone roaming work in Turkey?**
R: Turkey is NOT in the EU — free EU roaming does not apply. Your carrier will charge €3-15/day. An eSIM from Airalo costs €4-5 for 1GB/7 days — dramatically cheaper. Install before departure.

## Things to Do in Krakow: Complete 2026 Guide with Prices, Auschwitz & Insider Tips

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/experiente/things-to-do-krakow
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** experiente
**Publicat:** 2026-08-05
**Actualizat:** 2026-08-05
**Traducere a:** [ce-sa-faci-in-cracovia](https://plecari.com/ro/experiente/ce-sa-faci-in-cracovia)

**Descriere:** Complete Krakow 2026 guide — Wawel Castle, Kazimierz Jewish Quarter, Wieliczka Salt Mine, Auschwitz-Birkenau, Polish food, what's free, and a realistic budget. Europe's cheapest city break.

**Rezumat rapid:** Krakow deserves 3–4 days. Top priorities: Wawel Castle (grounds free, exhibitions €10–18), Kazimierz Jewish Quarter, Wieliczka Salt Mine 15km away (€33, must book online), and the Auschwitz-Birkenau day trip (70km, free entry but guided tour strongly recommended). Krakow is Central Europe's most affordable city break — pierogi €6–8, craft beer €2–3, 3-star hotel €30–60/night. Direct flight from Bucharest with Wizz Air, ~2h.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: How much does a 3-day city break in Krakow cost?**
R: Realistic budget per person: flights round-trip €60–120 (Wizz Air direct from Bucharest), 3 nights accommodation €90–180 (3-star hotel), attractions €80–100 (Wawel + Auschwitz + Wieliczka), food €40–60. Total: €270–460/person. Krakow is 40–50% cheaper than Prague or Vienna for equivalent experiences.

**Î: Do I need to book Auschwitz tickets in advance?**
R: Yes, mandatory in season (May–September). Entry to Auschwitz-Birkenau is free, but timed slots are limited and sell out 2–3 weeks ahead in summer. Book at auschwitz.org or via GetYourGuide. A guided tour (€35–45) is strongly recommended — the site covers 3km to Birkenau and historical context is essential.

**Î: Is Wieliczka Salt Mine worth visiting?**
R: Absolutely. The Wieliczka Salt Mine (UNESCO, 14km from Krakow) is one of Europe's most impressive underground attractions — 22 chambers carved entirely in salt, including St. Kinga's Chapel at 101m depth with chandeliers and bas-reliefs all made from salt. Standard tour 2–3h, €33/adult. Book online — in peak season tickets sell out 3–5 days ahead.

**Î: What's the best neighborhood in Krakow to stay?**
R: Old Town (Stare Miasto, within the ring road) is ideal for a first visit — everything is walkable. Kazimierz (the Jewish Quarter) offers more atmosphere, better restaurants, and prices 20% lower — perfect if you've been to Krakow before. Avoid the area around the central train station — far from attractions and less pleasant at night.

**Î: What's the currency in Poland — do they use euros?**
R: Poland uses the Polish Złoty (PLN). 1 EUR ≈ 4.30 PLN. Most places accept cards, but cash is sometimes cheaper. Avoid airport exchange offices — Kantor (currency exchange) offices in Kazimierz offer better rates. Never exchange at banks — commissions are high.

---

## Things to Do in Lisbon: Complete 2026 Guide with Prices, Alfama, Sintra & Insider Tips

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/experiente/things-to-do-lisbon
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** experiente
**Publicat:** 2026-08-06
**Actualizat:** 2026-08-06
**Traducere a:** [ce-sa-faci-in-lisabona](https://plecari.com/ro/experiente/ce-sa-faci-in-lisabona)

**Descriere:** Complete Lisbon 2026 guide — Alfama, Jerónimos Monastery, Belém, free miradouros, authentic fado, ginjinha, Sintra day trip. Important: Belém Tower closed for restoration in 2026.

**Rezumat rapid:** Lisbon deserves 3–4 days. Top priorities: Alfama and the historic neighborhoods (free, with fado in the evening), Jerónimos Monastery in Belém (~€18, book online), free miradouros at sunset, ginjinha at €1.50 a shot (mandatory), and the Sintra day trip (40 min by train, €2.45). Important 2026: Belém Tower is closed for restoration — photographable from outside but interior inaccessible. Lisbon is more expensive than Porto but offers unmatched neighborhood variety and energy.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: Is the Belém Tower open in 2026?**
R: No — Belém Tower is closed for restoration under Portugal's Recovery and Resilience Plan, with reopening expected sometime mid-2026 (date unconfirmed at time of writing). You can photograph the tower from the riverside promenade and surrounding gardens. Jerónimos Monastery, 500 meters away, is open and justifies the Belém trip on its own.

**Î: Lisbon or Porto — which should I visit first?**
R: Lisbon is the first choice for a first visit to Portugal — larger, more diverse, with multiple distinct neighborhoods (Alfama, Chiado, Bairro Alto, Belém, Parque das Nações), more theatrical fado, and Sintra 40 minutes away. Porto is more authentic, 20–30% cheaper, and has Port wine at source. Ideally you visit both — they're 3 hours apart by train.

**Î: What is the couvert in Portuguese restaurants?**
R: When you sit down, the waiter automatically brings bread, butter, olives, sometimes cheese or fish paste. These are NOT free — they appear on your bill (€2–5 per person). If you don't want them, decline immediately: 'Não, obrigado.' It's completely normal to refuse.

**Î: Is Tram 28 worth it or is it just for tourists?**
R: Tram 28 is a real public transport line that crosses Alfama and connects the historic neighborhoods — not a tourist attraction, but the tram locals used for decades. Worth it for atmosphere and the route through steep neighborhoods, but in summer it's packed with tourists. The alternative: bus 737 does the same route faster, with no queue.

**Î: Is Sintra worth a day trip?**
R: Yes, unconditionally — it's one of the most beautiful day trips in southern Europe. Train from Rossio in 40 minutes (€2.45 return) takes you to Sintra, with Pena Palace (pink and yellow on the mountain, €17), the National Palace (in the town center, €10), the Moorish Castle with mountain walls (€10), and Cabo da Roca — the westernmost point of continental Europe. Book Pena Palace online — it sells out weeks in advance.

---

## Things to Do in Ljubljana: Complete 2026 Guide with Prices, Lake Bled & Insider Tips

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/experiente/things-to-do-ljubljana
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** experiente
**Publicat:** 2026-08-05
**Actualizat:** 2026-08-05
**Traducere a:** [ce-sa-faci-in-ljubljana](https://plecari.com/ro/experiente/ce-sa-faci-in-ljubljana)

**Descriere:** Complete Ljubljana 2026 guide — Ljubljana Castle, Dragon Bridge, Metelkova, Lake Bled 1h away, Postojna Cave, Slovenian food, what's free. Europe's smallest and most surprising city break.

**Rezumat rapid:** Ljubljana deserves 2–3 days. Top priorities: Ljubljana Castle (free walk up, funicular €6, excellent views), Dragon Bridge and Prešeren Square (free), Metelkova alternative art district (free during the day), Lake Bled day trip (1h15 by bus, €6) and Postojna Cave (1h, €28). Ljubljana is compact, pedestrian-friendly, and genuinely surprising — an intact medieval center, excellent Slovenian food at accessible prices, and the Alps visible from the city center.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: How many days do you need in Ljubljana?**
R: 2 days comfortably cover the entire center: the Castle, Dragon Bridge, Prešeren Square, the riverbank, Metelkova, Tivoli Park. 3 days add a day trip to Lake Bled or Postojna Cave. 4 days allow both excursions plus Triglav National Park. Ljubljana is small — the advantage is that you're not rushing, you have time to stop at a riverside café.

**Î: Is Lake Bled worth the day trip from Ljubljana?**
R: Yes, absolutely — it's one of the most photogenic views in Europe. 1h15 by bus from Ljubljana (€6 return), Lake Bled has a small island with a white church in the center, a medieval castle on a cliff above the water, and the Slovenian Alps as backdrop. The original kremšnita cream cake (since 1953) is mandatory. In summer it gets crowded — arrive early.

**Î: Is Ljubljana expensive?**
R: No — it is 30–50% cheaper than Western European capitals. A main course at a local restaurant: €10–16. Ljubljana Castle (full ticket): ~€16. Public transport: free in the center with the Kavalir electric shuttle. Lake Bled by bus: €6. Ljubljana is cheaper than Vienna or Prague, but more expensive than Kraków or Sofia.

**Î: What is Metelkova and is it worth visiting?**
R: Metelkova is the former Yugoslav Army barracks, occupied in 1993 by artists and activists and transformed into the largest urban autonomous art zone in Europe. Buildings covered entirely with graffiti and art installations, alternative clubs, galleries, and a completely different energy from the tourist center. Daytime visit is free and interesting. Evenings (Thu–Sat) it becomes alternative nightlife. Not for everyone, but genuinely authentic.

**Î: How do I get from Bucharest to Ljubljana?**
R: No regular direct flight. The most efficient routes: fly to Venice (2h, Wizz Air/Ryanair) + bus or train to Ljubljana (2h30, ~€15–25). Or fly to Vienna (1h40) + Railjet train Vienna–Ljubljana (5h, €20–40). Or fly to Zagreb (1h) + bus Zagreb–Ljubljana (2h30, €8–15). Most accessible via Venice or Zagreb.

## Things to Do in Munich: Complete 2026 Guide with Prices, Oktoberfest & Neuschwanstein

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/experiente/things-to-do-munich
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** experiente
**Publicat:** 2026-08-06
**Actualizat:** 2026-08-06
**Traducere a:** [ce-sa-faci-in-munchen](https://plecari.com/ro/experiente/ce-sa-faci-in-munchen)

**Descriere:** Complete Munich 2026 guide — Marienplatz, English Garden with surfers, Nymphenburg Palace, Deutsches Museum, Bavarian beer gardens, Oktoberfest, and Neuschwanstein Castle day trip.

**Rezumat rapid:** Munich deserves 3–4 days. Top priorities: Marienplatz with the Glockenspiel (free), English Garden with the Eisbach surfers (free), Nymphenburg Palace (€15 full ticket), Deutsches Museum (€15), an evening at a local beer garden (€8–10 a litre), and the Neuschwanstein Castle day trip (€21 entry + train). Munich is expensive but has dozens of free attractions. Oktoberfest (September–October) transforms the city completely — book your hotel a year in advance.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: Is Munich expensive?**
R: Yes — Munich is one of Germany's most expensive cities and among Europe's priciest. 3-star hotel: €100–180/night, beer at Hofbräuhaus: €12–13/litre, traditional meal: €20–35. But it has dozens of free attractions (English Garden, Marienplatz, Viktualienmarkt, state museums at €1 on Sundays) and beer gardens where you can bring your own food and only pay for drinks. Realistic budget: €100–150/person/day.

**Î: Is Oktoberfest worth it if you don't drink beer?**
R: Surprisingly yes. Oktoberfest is more than beer — it's a folk festival with carousels, live music, authentic Bavarian food (rotisserie chicken, pork knuckle, giant pretzels), and a globally unique atmosphere. Entry to the festival grounds is free. You only pay for food and drink inside the tents. Without beer, your daily budget drops to €25–40 versus €60–100+ with drinks.

**Î: How do I get to Neuschwanstein Castle from Munich?**
R: Regional train (Regionalbahn) Munich–Füssen: ~2h, €21 return, or €29 with Bayern Ticket (covers up to 5 people — best value for groups). From Füssen, bus 73/78 to the castle (€4–6). Castle ticket: €21 adults — online booking mandatory months in advance in summer. Alternatively, an organised tour from Munich with transport included: €50–70.

**Î: When is Oktoberfest 2026?**
R: Oktoberfest 2026: September 19 – October 4, 2026. Dates vary annually — the first Saturday after September 15 is always opening day. Munich hotels during this period cost 3–5x the normal rate (€200–600/night for a 3-star). Book accommodation at least 6–12 months in advance.

**Î: What is the Bayern Ticket and how do I use it?**
R: Bayern Ticket is a regional train pass for Bavaria, valid for one day for 1–5 people at the same fixed price: €29/group (€26 digital). Covers all regional trains (not ICE/IC) in Bavaria Monday–Friday after 9:00 AM, all day on weekends. Perfect for Neuschwanstein (Füssen), Salzburg (Austria), or anywhere in Bavaria. One person pays €29, but 5 people also pay €29 — extremely efficient for groups.

---

## Things to Do in Paris 2026: Eiffel Tower, Louvre, Montmartre & the Art of Doing Nothing

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/experiente/things-to-do-paris
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** experiente
**Publicat:** 2026-07-15
**Actualizat:** 2026-07-15
